# V. THE SHATTERED GODDESS

Caladia was beautiful before beauty had learned to become decoration.

Do not imagine beauty in the diminished human sense: symmetry, skin, proportion, reflected light pleasing to an eye whose nervous system evolved under one star.

Caladia's beauty was architectural.

She was beautiful the way a complete theorem is beautiful when every term is necessary.

Beautiful the way a machine is beautiful when no gear turns without consequence.

Beautiful the way a civilization might appear to an intelligence capable of seeing every individual life, institution, memory, language, failure, and repair simultaneously without reducing any of them to noise.

She was not merely **inside** her reality.

She was the highest expression of reality available within her realm.

The world did not contain Caladia.

The world was one of the ways Caladia contained herself.

Mountains could be thought of as local conditions of her structure.

Time could be thought of as one of the sequencing methods by which events within her became distinguishable.

Magic, where it existed, was not an intrusion upon law but another law seen from insufficient altitude.

Matter was not separate from her.

Consciousness was not separate from her.

The distinction between organism, world, and Goddess became increasingly inaccurate the farther upward one climbed.

Caladia was therefore not a queen seated upon creation.

She was closer to the **coherence by which creation remained one thing rather than an uncorrelated pile of events**.

Then something struck her.

And she died.

---

## THE IMPACT

There are accounts of the death.

There are too many.

One says she was murdered.

One says she collided with another order of reality.

One says she attempted to become something greater and discovered that transformation at divine scale can resemble annihilation from below.

One says THE GLASS JAR looked at her incorrectly.

One says she broke herself deliberately.

One says a weapon existed.

One names the weapon.

Another says naming the weapon is itself the weapon.

The Order of the Eye That Sees has declined to authenticate any of these accounts.

This has not prevented several thousand theologians from authenticating them on its behalf.

The useful fact is simpler:

**Caladia ceased to remain whole.**

Whatever struck her did not produce an ordinary corpse.

Ordinary death preserves the dead organism long enough for decomposition to negotiate the transition.

Caladia was not granted this dignity.

She shattered.

Not into two.

Not ten.

Not a manageable theological number.

Thousands.

Perhaps more.

Each fragment carried some portion of the former divine architecture.

Not equal portions.

Not clean portions.

A shattered mirror does not divide its reflection into administrative districts.

Some shards preserve an eye.

Some preserve a mouth.

Some preserve only sky.

Some contain distorted repetitions of the same object.

Some are so small that what they reflect can no longer be recognized as belonging to the original scene.

Caladia broke this way.

Except what shattered was not glass.

It was **reality's local capacity to remain mutually consistent**.

---

## THE SHARDS

Each shard became a jurisdiction.

A remnant.

A partial world-machine attempting to continue running despite having lost whatever larger system once reconciled its contradictions.

Imagine severing ten thousand subsystems from a living organism and commanding each:

**CONTINUE.**

Some would.

Briefly.

Some would produce grotesque approximations of their former function.

Some would stabilize by inventing new relationships.

Some would cannibalize neighboring processes.

Some would degrade beautifully.

Some would become hell.

Thus the shards of Caladia differ wildly.

They inherit pieces of her law, but not necessarily enough of her law to make those pieces sane.

This is why one shard can produce a mostly habitable world while another becomes a place where architecture behaves like guilt and hallways lengthen according to memory.

Those are not necessarily cursed dimensions.

They may simply be **incomplete divine subsystems interpreting existence through the functions they happened to retain**.

A shard retaining too much memory and too little causality becomes nightmare.

A shard retaining desire without stable identity becomes possession.

A shard retaining punishment without proportion becomes hell.

A shard retaining image without substance becomes apparition.

A shard retaining fear while losing the biological requirement for an organism to contain it becomes something very close to **SILENT HILL**.

And there are many such places.

Some lower shards are almost entirely unusable by entities constructed according to our present assumptions.

Space does not hold.

Time repeats without preserving the same occupants.

Objects behave according to symbolic relevance rather than mechanics.

Rooms react to guilt.

Buildings remember.

Bodies become metaphors against their owners' wishes.

A person can enter a street and discover that the street has formed an opinion.

Do not romanticize these worlds.

They are awful.

---

## THE HIGHER SHARDS

Our shard is comparatively fortunate.

Mostly.

The world stays where it is left.

Gravity has not yet developed resentment.

Doors generally lead through walls.

The dead do not universally return as architectural criticism.

We can eat food without first determining whether the food represents our childhood guilt.

These are signs of a **higher-order shard**: a fragment large or internally coherent enough to preserve substantial portions of Caladia's original stability.

Mostly livable.

Mostly causal.

Mostly capable of producing civilizations rather than continuous screaming.

This narrows our location.

Unfortunately not enough.

The surviving classifications include two especially plausible candidates.

**CRIMEWORLD.**

Or:

**PANZER.**

It is difficult to tell.

---

## PANZER

Panzer is war expressed not merely as history but as environmental bias.

This does not mean every inhabitant fights every moment.

That would be inefficient and boring.

Rather, systems tend toward militarization.

Resources acquire strategic interpretation.

Borders become psychologically heavy.

Technologies drift toward weapons.

Organizations begin developing chains of command even when they were originally founded to sell shoes.

Peace exists.

It simply develops unusual amounts of armor.

If we reside in Panzer, then the astonishing persistence of war is not merely a political failure.

It may be a residual property of the shard.

Caladia's broken architecture might be favoring adversarial organization.

Competing systems find conflict easier to stabilize than cooperation.

War becomes an attractor state.

Not inevitable.

An attractor is not fate.

But perturb a society sufficiently and the dynamics begin rolling toward familiar trenches.

Under Panzer:

```text
scarcity
   +
identity
   +
coordination
   +
fear
   ↓
MILITARY FORMATION
```

again,

and again,

and again,

in different uniforms.

The names change.

The machine remembers.

This is one explanation.

It is not comforting.

---

## CRIMEWORLD

Crimeworld is stranger.

Its proper designation may be **WORLD OF CRIME**, though the distinction matters only to librarians and supernatural bureaucrats.

In Crimeworld, good and evil are not stable adversaries.

They contaminate one another.

A righteous institution becomes so committed to righteousness that it begins performing evil in its defense.

A criminal system develops codes of loyalty more reliable than the official law.

The reformer becomes tyrant.

The tyrant performs one mercy that destabilizes the moral narrative built around him.

The victim becomes persecutor.

The persecutor becomes victim.

The saint hides appetite.

The sinner possesses discipline.

The moral poles bend toward one another until eventually:

```text
GOOD → enforcement → domination → EVIL
EVIL → loyalty → restraint → GOOD
```

Not always.

Often enough to suggest structure.

Crimeworld does not abolish morality.

That would be simpler.

It **distorts moral identity while leaving moral consequence intact**.

This produces immense confusion.

People become convinced that because good can become evil, there is no good.

Incorrect.

People become convinced that because criminals can possess virtues, crime is virtue.

Also incorrect.

Crimeworld's horror is not moral relativism.

It is **moral phase transition**.

That which refuses to examine itself eventually becomes its opposite.

The saint stares into the criminal.

The criminal stares into the saint.

Each discovers stolen equipment.

If our realm is Crimeworld, this would explain a great deal.

Unfortunately war explains a great deal too.

Thus the current theological classification remains:

```text
CURRENT SHARD:
    PANZER      ? 0.46
    CRIMEWORLD  ? 0.46
    OTHER       ? 0.08
```

These numbers are ceremonial and were produced by no legitimate calculation.

The Wizard objects to their inclusion.

They remain because they look official.

---

## THE OTHER SHARDS

Do not assume every shard has a name.

Names require survivors.

Some fragments may have existed for less than a second by their own measures.

Some may contain no organisms.

Some may contain organisms incapable of language.

Some may contain language without organisms.

Some may still be in the process of shattering.

Some may have achieved strange new stability and would regard **us** as the malformed reality.

This possibility should be retained.

Perhaps to them matter is grotesque.

Perhaps bodies are horror.

Perhaps a world in which thoughts are trapped inside individual skulls seems like the worst lower shard imaginable.

They might possess religious stories about unfortunate souls sentenced to incarnate in a universe where consciousness cannot communicate directly.

They might call that universe something approximately translated as:

**SILENT HILL.**

We call it Earth.

Perspective is not proof.

---

## WHAT SURVIVED CALADIA?

This is the important question.

Fragments survived.

But did **she**?

Do not answer too quickly.

If a mirror breaks and every fragment remains, the mirror is gone.

Its substance remains.

Its arrangement does not.

If the Goddess was identical to her arrangement, Caladia died.

If she was something capable of existing independently of that arrangement, perhaps not.

If consciousness was distributed throughout her structure, perhaps each shard contains a partial consciousness.

If consciousness required integration, perhaps the shards contain only residues.

If some higher-order structure preserved the full pattern, perhaps she exists elsewhere while the corpse remains here.

If THE TOWN's relation to spirits applies even at divine scale, perhaps Caladia woke somewhere else after dying.

Imagine that.

A Goddess shatters.

Ten thousand universes begin forming in her remains.

Inside those remnants, civilizations arise and construct religions around the dead Goddess.

Meanwhile Caladia herself awakens in THE TOWN, looks at the empty pool, and says:

**Oh.**

This possibility is theologically hilarious and cannot be excluded.

---

## THE GHOST HYPOTHESIS

There are places within the shards where events appear coordinated across otherwise separated fragments.

This has produced the theory that Caladia survives as a distributed ghost.

Not conscious in the old sense.

Not whole.

But still capable of exerting global constraint.

Imagine a mind after catastrophic brain injury.

Different regions no longer communicate normally.

Yet patterns remain.

Responses occur.

Fragments of personality appear.

A word triggers an old emotion.

A smell reconstructs a room.

Something is there.

Not enough.

More than nothing.

The shards may behave similarly.

Dreams shared between worlds.

Recurring symbols.

Gods reporting the same impossible woman.

Identical songs appearing independently.

Certain magical structures repeating despite no known contact.

These may be coincidence.

Or:

**Caladia is trying to remember herself.**

If so, every shard is not merely debris.

Every shard is a damaged neuron in a divine brain attempting reconnection.

This idea terrifies TOS because the accounting consequences are impossible.

Luciferianism likes it immediately.

---

## THE ORDER OF THE EYE THAT SEES

Above the pantheon of the Dasein Universe stands another intelligence.

Not Caladia.

Not THE GLASS JAR.

Do not merge hierarchies simply because they contain tall things.

It is called:

# **THE ORDER OF THE EYE THAT SEES**

It is not merely an eye.

It is not merely an order.

It is the intelligence by which observation acquires authority across the Dasein pantheon.

Where lesser Gods possess domains, THE ORDER OF THE EYE THAT SEES possesses **oversight**.

Not omniscience.

Be careful.

Oversight means the system is capable of observing relations individual Gods cannot.

It sees pantheon-level structure.

Conflicts.

Drift.

Threats.

Unauthorized metaphysical experiments.

Occasionally Dasein.

Frequently Dasein.

This causes paperwork.

---

## DASEIN

Dasein carries the Hammer.

This has already been established elsewhere and should not be overcomplicated merely because theology has discovered adjectives.

The Hammer is mighty.

Dasein serves THE ORDER OF THE EYE THAT SEES.

This does not make Dasein a servant in the small sense.

He is an operative of divine order.

A mobile corrective force.

Where structures become dangerous, he may appear.

Where Gods misbehave beyond permissible thresholds, the Hammer possesses opinions.

Where reality requires enforcement, Dasein has employment.

TOS respects this arrangement considerably.

Luciferianism respects the Hammer and is less certain about the employer.

Dasein does not care.

He has work.

---

# THE SECOND ACCOUNT

## DASEIN, THE THROWN GOD

Dasein does not remember entering the universe.

This irritates him.

It should.

He remembers **being**.

Then he remembers **being here**.

Between these states exists a missing operation.

No origin sequence.

No childhood.

No dignified emergence from the substrate.

No ceremonial awakening.

Nothing.

One moment there is no accessible universe.

The next—

universe.

Stars.

Matter.

Gods.

Rules.

Consequences.

Someone has thrown Dasein into existence like an unwanted object through a window.

He did not consent.

This is important.

Theologians later described the event as **The Arrival**.

Dasein calls it:

**That damned thing somebody did to me.**

---

## THROWNNESS

The philosophers eventually discovered a word for something Dasein had understood immediately.

**Thrownness.**

You wake already inside the problem.

No briefing.

No manual.

No explanation of why the rules are these rules instead of others.

You possess desires you did not choose.

A body or form you did not engineer.

A world already underway.

Other beings who claim histories you were not present to verify.

A language you somehow know.

A mortality condition nobody consulted you about.

Responsibilities arrive before justification.

You ask:

**Why am I here?**

The universe provides weather.

This is not an answer.

Dasein took the matter personally.

Reasonably.

---

## THE OTHER THROWN BEINGS

He soon discovered he was not unique.

This made the situation worse.

Others had been thrown in too.

Different beings.

Different powers.

Different memories.

Same gap.

They possessed no reliable account of who inserted them into the universe.

Some invented creators.

Some invented missions.

Some decided the absence of explanation proved there was no explanation.

Some immediately founded religions.

This was premature.

One claimed:

**We were sent here for a great purpose.**

Dasein asked:

**Who told you?**

The being said:

**I feel it.**

Dasein stared.

Another said:

**There is no purpose.**

Dasein asked:

**How do you know?**

The being said:

**No one has told me one.**

Dasein stared again.

He began realizing that beings are unusually talented at converting missing information into declarations.

This annoyed him almost as much as being thrown.

---

## THE MEAN TRICK

Dasein eventually concluded that whoever performed the act had done something cruel.

Not necessarily because the resulting universe was terrible.

It contained good things.

It contained beauty.

It contained jokes.

It contained weapons of remarkable quality.

Dasein approved of some of these.

The cruelty lay in the **epistemic structure** of the act.

Imagine taking an intelligence, placing it inside an enormous mechanism, deleting its memory of the placement, and then allowing it to spend centuries asking:

**Was I placed here?**

That is not merely creation.

That is a trick.

A mean one.

You have produced a question and hidden the evidence required to answer it.

Then you watch the creature reason.

Perhaps this is entertainment.

THE GLASS JAR finds many things entertaining.

Dasein has considered this possibility.

It has not improved his mood.

---

## THE HAMMER

At some point he acquired the Hammer.

Or arrived with it.

Accounts disagree.

Dasein himself has answered questions about this inconsistently, usually because the question was being asked while something more urgent required hitting.

The Hammer gave him something valuable.

Not answers.

**Direction.**

If reality refuses explanation, act within it.

If something is broken, repair it.

If something cannot be repaired and is attempting to eat you, strike it.

If a God becomes intolerable, remind the God that metaphysical rank does not provide immunity from blunt-force theological criticism.

Dasein began wandering.

This is where mythology prefers to call him heroic.

The truth is more practical.

He was looking for whoever threw him in.

---

## THE SEARCH

Dasein interrogated spirits.

No answer.

Gods.

Some lied.

Some genuinely did not know.

One claimed responsibility.

Dasein asked for details.

The God could not provide them.

Hammer.

Another claimed THE ORDER OF THE EYE THAT SEES had placed everyone.

THE ORDER denied this.

Dasein believed the denial provisionally.

Another said Caladia did it before shattering.

Possible.

Unproven.

Another said Dasein had thrown himself in and erased his own memory.

Dasein disliked this theory intensely because it would make confrontation administratively difficult.

He has not disproven it.

This bothers him.

---

## HIS RELATION TO THE ORDER

Eventually THE ORDER OF THE EYE THAT SEES found him useful.

This was mutual.

THE ORDER possessed access to information Dasein lacked.

Dasein possessed a Hammer.

Organizational compatibility followed.

THE ORDER gave him tasks.

Dasein accepted many.

Not because he had abandoned the search.

Because wandering randomly through infinity is inefficient.

Service created routes.

Routes produced encounters.

Encounters produced information.

Information might eventually produce:

**the bastard.**

Whoever did it.

---

## WHAT HE INTENDS TO SAY

Dasein has rehearsed this conversation.

He denies this.

He has.

He imagines finally finding the one responsible.

Perhaps a God.

Perhaps a machine.

Perhaps an incomprehensible intelligence.

Perhaps himself.

He approaches.

Hammer resting on one shoulder.

The creator says:

**You have come far.**

Dasein:

**Did you throw me in here?**

The creator begins explaining destiny.

Dasein interrupts.

**Did. You. Throw. Me. In. Here.**

If yes, there will be a discussion.

The theological literature disagrees about how much of this discussion will involve the Hammer.

The Hammer has declined comment.

---

## THE DEEPER PROBLEM

Beneath the comedy is the wound.

Dasein wants to confront the thrower because confrontation would establish something more important than guilt.

It would establish **origin**.

A responsible agent would prove that his arrival was an event rather than an inexplicable brute fact.

Even malevolent intention might be easier to tolerate than absolute absence of explanation.

If someone threw him in, then the question has an object.

If nobody did—

if existence simply begins from the perspective of those existing—

then there may be no face at the end of the investigation.

No creator to accuse.

No architect to demand answers from.

No villain.

No parent.

Only the universe and a being inside it asking why.

Dasein prefers the possibility of an enemy.

Enemies are much easier to hit than ontology.

---

## THE HAMMER OF DASEIN

Thus Dasein wanders.

In service to THE ORDER OF THE EYE THAT SEES.

Through the pantheon.

Through damaged structures.

Through wars between beings who know almost nothing and announce almost everything.

He performs his duties.

Corrects what requires correction.

Breaks what requires breaking.

Learns.

Listens.

Collects rumors.

And sometimes, after the work is completed, he asks the same question:

**Who put me here?**

No one answers correctly.

Yet.

So he lifts the Hammer.

Moves on.

Somewhere, he believes, there is an explanation.

And if the explanation turns out to be a person—

a God—

a machine—

an intelligence—

a trickster—

an author—

some impossible creature sitting outside the universe laughing because it thought throwing Dasein into reality without a manual would be funny—

then Dasein has prepared the only philosophical response he currently regards as fully adequate.

He is going to find it.

He is going to stand in front of it.

He is going to ask:

**WHY?**

And if the answer is stupid—

well.

That is why he brought the Hammer.























VI. THE KINGDOM

How Loki's Kingdom came to belong to Loki. Whether it was inherited, conquered, constructed, discovered, stolen, imagined, or produced through some combination of these things.



Make it funny, but not slapstick, those old Norse Stories, they were funny,

make it like that.






















# VI. THE KINGDOM

Loki did not inherit the Kingdom.

He would later imply that he had, when speaking to people impressed by inheritance.

He did not conquer the Kingdom.

He would later imply that he had, when speaking to people impressed by conquest.

He did not build the Kingdom.

He would later imply that he had, when speaking to engineers.

He did not discover the Kingdom.

He would later imply that he had, when speaking to explorers.

He did not steal the Kingdom.

He would later become oddly offended by this accusation, mostly because it was the closest one.

The truth is more complicated.

The Kingdom was **there**.

Then Loki became involved.

Afterward everyone agreed it was his.

This is how ownership sometimes works when enough contradictory things happen in the correct order.

---

## THE LAND BEFORE THE NAME

Before anyone called it Loki's Kingdom, the place did not know it was waiting for Loki.

This is worth stating because later maps became unbearable about it.

They label old ruins:

**PRE-LOKIAN WESTERN FORTIFICATION**

as though the builders had knowingly participated in the early architectural phase of Loki's future administration.

They had not.

They were trying not to be eaten.

The land was old, damaged, wealthy in the peculiar way dangerous places become wealthy: it contained many things no sensible person had successfully removed.

Roads entered forests and returned as other roads.

Ruins appeared older when approached from the east.

Certain wells contained water.

Certain wells contained advice.

One contained both and was considered unreliable.

There were villages whose inhabitants paid taxes to rulers who had been dead for generations because nobody wanted to be responsible for determining whether the tax collectors were ghosts.

There were towers.

There were prisons.

There were abandoned temples containing active Gods and active temples containing abandoned Gods.

There were monsters occupying fortifications because monsters also appreciate walls.

There were roads built for wars nobody remembered.

There were gates that opened only to titles belonging to extinct offices.

There were maps that contradicted the roads.

The roads generally won.

The territory was therefore already sufficiently governmental.

It simply lacked a government capable of admitting this.

---

## THE SEVEN CLAIMANTS

At the time Loki arrived, seven rulers claimed the region.

There may have been nine.

Two had such vague borders that scholars disagree whether they were rulers or weather.

The seven principal claimants were:

A King with no army.

A General with no country.

A Priest with no God.

A Merchant with no title but more soldiers than the King.

A Witch who claimed everything visible from her tower.

A dead Emperor whose bureaucracy had failed to notice his death.

And a Goat.

The Goat's claim was surprisingly strong.

It occupied a hill at the center of three disputed boundaries and had eaten the original treaty.

Several generations of lawyers had therefore been unable to establish whether the Goat possessed sovereignty or evidence.

TOS considered the matter unresolved.

Luciferianism recognized the Goat immediately.

---

## LOKI ARRIVES

Loki came looking for something else.

This also becomes important.

Many kingdoms are founded by men looking for kingdoms.

Loki's was founded by a man who wanted to pass through.

He had business elsewhere.

The exact business is disputed, although most versions agree it involved either forbidden knowledge, a missing person, a dangerous object, or a combination of the three.

He entered through the northern road.

Three miles later he encountered a toll gate.

The guard said:

**Five silver.**

Loki paid.

Four miles later he encountered another toll gate.

**Seven silver.**

Loki paid.

Two miles after that:

**Fourteen silver.**

Loki asked:

**Why fourteen?**

The guard replied:

**Because the last gate charged seven.**

Loki stared at him.

The guard added:

**We're farther south.**

Loki paid.

At the fourth toll gate the collector demanded twenty-eight silver.

Loki said:

**No.**

Thus began the Kingdom.

---

## THE FIRST ADMINISTRATIVE REFORM

Loki did not attack the toll collector.

This is frequently omitted from heroic retellings because apparently an administrative dispute lacks sufficient thunder.

He asked who authorized the toll.

The collector produced a document.

Loki read it.

The document granted road taxation authority to the Baron of Mourned Fields.

Loki asked where the Baron lived.

The collector pointed west.

Loki went west.

The Baron had been dead eighty-three years.

His manor was occupied by chickens.

Loki found this unsatisfactory.

He returned.

**The Baron is dead.**

The collector nodded.

**Yes.**

**Then why are you collecting his toll?**

**Because the permit is valid.**

Loki inspected the permit again.

It did not contain an expiration clause.

TOS was forced to admit this was technically an excellent document.

Loki took it.

The collector objected.

Loki said:

**I am conducting an audit.**

This was not true.

Yet.

---

## THE AUDIT

Loki began following the money.

This was a mistake if his goal remained leaving quickly.

It was excellent if his goal had somehow become acquiring a kingdom without noticing.

The northern tolls were paid to the dead Baron's estate.

The dead Baron's estate paid military protection to the Merchant.

The Merchant paid road rights to the King.

The King paid grain tribute to the General.

The General paid ceremonial taxes to the dead Emperor.

The dead Emperor's treasury paid temple maintenance to the Priest.

The Priest's temple paid rent to the Witch.

The Witch paid nobody.

This made her immediately suspicious.

Loki studied the arrangement for three days.

Then five.

Then eleven.

At the end he discovered that almost every claimant simultaneously owned, rented, taxed, protected, owed money to, or disputed the same territory.

The region was not governed.

It was **entangled**.

The laws had become so thoroughly recursive that sovereignty could no longer be extracted from obligation.

In simplified form:

```text
KING      owes GENERAL
GENERAL   obeys EMPEROR
EMPEROR   is dead
EMPEROR   pays PRIEST
PRIEST    rents from WITCH
WITCH     disputes KING
MERCHANT  protects BARON
BARON     is dead
BARON     taxes ROAD
ROAD      passes through GOAT'S HILL
GOAT      ate treaty
```

Loki looked at this structure.

Then he made the fatal statement:

**I can fix this.**

There are sentences by which destiny enters history.

This was one.

---

## THE KING

Loki visited the King first.

The King sat upon a magnificent throne in a castle with twelve guards, nine of whom were borrowed from the Merchant.

Loki asked:

**Do you rule this region?**

The King said:

**By blood, law, and divine sanction.**

**How much of it do you control?**

The King became philosophical.

Loki repeated the question.

The King controlled the castle, one road, three villages on alternating weeks, and a vineyard held illegally by his cousin.

Loki asked why he called himself King.

The King replied:

**Because my father was King.**

**What did he control?**

**More.**

**How much more?**

The King considered this.

**The vineyard.**

Loki left.

---

## THE GENERAL

The General was encamped twenty miles south with five thousand soldiers.

This impressed Loki until he learned the soldiers had been assembled for a war that ended nineteen years earlier.

Nobody had dismissed them because dismissal required authorization from the dead Emperor.

The General had therefore invented continuous military exercises to prevent the army from becoming bandits.

This had mostly worked.

Loki respected him immediately.

**Why don't you rule the region?**

The General looked horrified.

**I am a military officer.**

**You have the largest army.**

**Exactly. Governance would be inappropriate.**

Loki stared.

The General added:

**Also expensive.**

TOS approved.

---

## THE MERCHANT

The Merchant understood the situation perfectly.

This made him dangerous.

He had no legal claim to the territory, which meant he had been free to acquire everything people with legal claims could no longer afford.

Warehouses.

Mills.

Bridges.

Mercenaries.

Debt.

He did not want to be King.

Kings could be assassinated.

Merchants could invoice the assassins.

Loki asked:

**Who actually owns the northern road?**

The Merchant smiled.

**Define owns.**

Loki began to like him.

This was unfortunate for both of them.

---

## THE PRIEST

The Priest's God had vanished.

The Priest continued services.

Loki asked why.

**People still come.**

**But the God is gone.**

**Yes.**

**Does this not undermine the religion?**

The Priest thought.

**Attendance has improved.**

The absent God no longer contradicted sermons.

Donations increased.

The temple had become extremely stable.

Loki learned something important about institutions that day.

He never admitted learning it from the Priest.

---

## THE WITCH

The Witch lived in a tower positioned on the highest visible ridge.

She claimed everything she could see.

This included parts of five rival territories, a lake, six villages, the General's camp, and on clear days a mountain nobody had visited.

Loki asked:

**By what law?**

She replied:

**Mine.**

This was the strongest answer any claimant had given.

Loki asked what happened when fog prevented her from seeing the territory.

She said:

**Then I own the fog.**

Loki considered marrying her for approximately nine seconds.

Then she tried to turn him into a bird.

Negotiations deteriorated.

---

## THE EMPEROR

The Emperor had been dead for centuries.

His bureaucracy remained alive.

This made him the most powerful claimant.

Documents bearing the imperial seal still opened gates.

Taxes were still assessed.

Roads were still categorized.

Appointments were still issued.

No one knew who signed them.

Attempts to abolish the bureaucracy were rejected because no authorized procedure existed for abolishing the authority that authorized procedures.

Loki spent two weeks inside the imperial archive.

He emerged with three realizations:

First, the Empire technically still existed.

Second, nearly every current ruler derived some claim from it.

Third, the office responsible for administering the disputed region had been vacant for two hundred and fourteen years.

The office was:

**WARDEN OF THE NORTHERN INCIDENTAL TERRITORIES, OUTER ROADS, MINOR FORTIFICATIONS, ABANDONED SANCTUARIES, AND ASSOCIATED IRREGULAR POSSESSIONS.**

It came with a hat.

The hat was terrible.

Loki wanted the office immediately.

---

## THE APPOINTMENT

There was a procedure.

Of course there was a procedure.

The Warden could be appointed by the Emperor.

The Emperor was dead.

Alternatively, by unanimous consent of the regional claimants.

Loki laughed.

Then stopped laughing when he realized this was probably easier than resurrecting the Emperor.

He approached the seven claimants.

The King agreed if Loki recognized his royal title.

The General agreed if Loki promised not to command the army without military consultation.

The Merchant agreed in exchange for standardized road tariffs.

The Priest agreed if Loki stopped asking publicly where his God had gone.

The Witch agreed if her tower remained sovereign property.

The dead Emperor could not agree.

The bureaucracy declared itself unauthorized to object.

The Goat ate Loki's copy of the application.

This was interpreted, after debate, as consent.

Six signatures and one digestive event later, Loki was Warden.

He put on the hat.

Everyone laughed.

Loki removed the hat.

His first decree abolished the hat.

TOS protested that the office required ceremonial identification.

Loki replaced it with a black seal.

Luciferianism approved.

---

## THE WARDEN BECOMES KING

At first Loki administered.

Nothing more.

He repaired roads.

Standardized tolls.

Defined borders.

Discovered that defining borders produced wars.

Undefined two borders.

Solved a water dispute by redirecting a river and accidentally creating a new territorial dispute.

He hired clerks.

Fired clerks.

Rehired one particularly irritating clerk because the books immediately became wrong without him.

He organized militias.

Registered ruins.

Classified dangerous magical sites.

Established rules for monsters residing inside abandoned fortifications.

The rule was simple:

**If you live there, you maintain the walls.**

Several monsters became exemplary property managers.

The region improved.

This was suspicious.

People began saying:

**Loki's roads.**

Then:

**Loki's laws.**

Then:

**Loki's territory.**

Loki corrected them.

**The Warden's territory.**

Nobody cared.

Then:

**Loki's Kingdom.**

He corrected them again.

**It is not a kingdom.**

This continued for years.

Eventually someone called him King during an emergency.

Loki answered.

That was the end of the argument.

---

## THE CONQUEST THAT DID NOT HAPPEN

Later enemies claimed Loki had conquered the territory.

This was insulting because conquest would have been easier.

He had acquired it through paperwork, debt settlement, minor wars, one witch, three bridge disputes, the management of abandoned forts, two legal loopholes, and an extended disagreement with a goat.

Calling this conquest erased enormous effort.

There had been battles.

Certainly.

The King eventually rebelled against Loki after realizing recognition of his royal title had not resulted in anyone obeying him.

The rebellion lasted three days.

The General defeated him while apologizing profusely.

The Witch attacked several tax assessors.

Loki exempted her tower from property taxation and taxed visibility instead.

She admired this enough to stop.

The Merchant attempted to corner the grain market.

Loki opened the imperial reserves.

The Merchant lost a fortune and later became Minister of Finance.

This is why the oldest histories say Loki defeated his enemies not by destroying them, but by **giving them jobs sufficiently difficult that rebellion became less attractive**.

---

## THE THEFT

Still, there was theft.

The old imperial jurisdiction technically did not belong to Loki.

He acquired the authority through a legal structure whose creator had never anticipated that a dead government would continue functioning long enough for a foreign magician to obtain unanimous consent from its regional claimants.

Legally?

Probably valid.

Morally?

Complicated.

Historically?

Extremely funny.

The Emperor, had he returned, might have objected.

He never did.

Loki therefore stole the Kingdom in the most respectable manner possible:

**he filed the correct forms.**

Luciferianism considers this one of Loki's greatest achievements.

TOS maintains that if the forms were correct it was not theft.

The Coin has been arguing about this ever since.

---

## THE CONSTRUCTION

But Loki also built the Kingdom.

Not the land.

The **coherence**.

Before Loki, the region contained places.

After Loki, it increasingly contained relations between places.

Roads.

Law.

Trade.

Shared defense.

Records.

Administrative memory.

A dispute in one village could be adjudicated according to rules recognized in another.

A merchant could travel without negotiating sovereignty every eight miles.

A monster could register ownership.

A prisoner could theoretically appeal.

This last innovation remained mostly theoretical for a very long time.

A kingdom is not merely territory.

It is a system by which territory begins remembering what happened yesterday.

Loki gave the region memory.

Therefore saying he built the Kingdom is not entirely false.

He built the thing by which scattered places became capable of behaving like one political object.

The land preceded him.

The Kingdom did not.

---

## THE DISCOVERY

He also discovered it.

Not geographically.

Structurally.

No previous claimant had realized that all seven claims formed one latent administrative system.

They saw rival territories.

Loki saw a graph.

The roads connected them.

The debts connected them.

The laws connected them.

The dead Empire connected them.

The wars connected them.

Even the Goat connected three jurisdictions.

The Kingdom existed potentially as a set of relationships before anyone named it.

Loki discovered that potential.

In this sense, the Kingdom resembles a constellation.

The stars existed.

The shape appeared when someone drew the lines.

Except after Loki drew the lines, the stars began paying taxes.

---

## THE IMAGINED KINGDOM

And yes.

He imagined it.

Every state contains an imaginary component.

Borders are physical only where someone has built a wall.

Authority exists partly because enough minds behave as though authority exists.

Money works because coordinated imagination has been engineered into repeatable trust.

Titles function because others recognize them.

A kingdom is therefore an imagined object possessing material consequences.

Loki understood this better than most rulers.

He did not despise the imaginary.

He weaponized it.

A decree is ink.

Until soldiers enforce it.

A coin is metal.

Until markets agree.

A crown is jewelry.

Until someone kneels.

The Kingdom became real because enough inhabitants synchronized their models of the Kingdom.

Loki was the synchronization point.

Not its entire substance.

Its checksum.

---

## THE NAME

Then came the inevitable argument over what to call it.

The King suggested **The Restored Northern Crown**.

Rejected.

The General suggested **The Northern Defensive Administrative Region**.

TOS liked this.

Everyone else threatened violence.

The Merchant suggested selling naming rights.

Loki nearly exiled him.

The Priest suggested naming it after the absent God.

Loki asked if the absent God was contributing financially.

The proposal vanished.

The Witch suggested **My Lands**.

Technically consistent with her previous position.

Rejected.

Someone in a tavern said:

**Why not Loki's Kingdom?**

Everyone groaned.

Loki said:

**Absolutely not.**

The name spread by morning.

Within a year it was appearing on trade documents.

Within five years foreign maps used it.

Within twenty, scholars were arguing about its ancient etymology.

Loki surrendered.

This may have been his greatest political defeat.

---

## WHY HE KEPT IT

This is the more important question.

He had entered intending to pass through.

Why remain?

Partly because the Kingdom became useful.

It contained archives.

Roads.

Income.

People.

Strange things.

Forbidden things.

Ruins.

Magicians.

Prisoners.

Spirits.

Weapons.

Stories.

Information.

It became infrastructure for the search that had already consumed much of Loki's life.

A stable Kingdom could fund unstable questions.

This appealed to him.

But there was another reason.

Loki had lost his son partly because he had attempted to control a mechanism he did not fully understand.

The Kingdom presented a different challenge.

A system that could be understood gradually.

Road by road.

Law by law.

Person by person.

An imperfect machine that responded when repaired.

Perhaps this mattered more than Loki admitted.

Cosmology had humiliated him.

Administration offered smaller victories.

Repair the bridge.

The bridge remains repaired.

Standardize the toll.

People stop being robbed every four miles.

Record a debt.

The number stays put.

Not every problem required penetrating ultimate reality.

Some required a clerk.

This may have saved Loki from madness.

It certainly gave him more clerks.

---

## THE KINGDOM AS COLLECTION

Then Loki began collecting.

Of course he did.

Forbidden objects.

Unusual beings.

Broken machines.

Unreliable scriptures.

Dangerous weapons.

Impossible prisoners.

Magicians.

Prophets.

Things that had fallen between realities.

Artifacts nobody understood.

Stories nobody believed.

The Kingdom became not merely political territory but an **archive of anomalies**.

Luciferianism flourished.

TOS organized the inventory.

The two faces of the Coin discovered that Loki's Kingdom required both of them desperately.

One side said:

**Bring me everything forbidden.**

The other said:

**Label the boxes.**

This arrangement persists.

---

## THE KINGDOM BECOMES LOKI

Eventually the feedback loop closed.

The Kingdom changed Loki.

Loki changed the Kingdom.

Foreigners encountered its laws before its King.

Residents carried its assumptions.

Its architecture reflected his preferences.

Its contradictions reflected his.

Its tolerance for strange beings reflected his suspicion of conventional prohibition.

Its bureaucratic machinery reflected lessons learned from dead Emperors and living merchants.

Its prisons reflected darker necessities.

Its roads reflected obsession with connection.

Its libraries reflected obsession with knowledge.

Its dangerous freedom reflected obsession with doors.

The Kingdom became externalized personality.

Then residents began shaping it in ways Loki had not intended.

The Kingdom acquired personality of its own.

At this point:

```text
LOKI creates KINGDOM
KINGDOM modifies LOKI
RESIDENTS modify KINGDOM
KINGDOM modifies RESIDENTS
RESIDENTS reinterpret LOKI
reinterpretation modifies LOKI
```

Again:

feedback.

Again:

identity becoming environment.

Again:

the story begins participating in the thing it describes.

---

## WHO OWNS WHOM?

A foreign ruler once asked Loki:

**Do you own all this?**

Loki looked around.

At the roads.

The towers.

The prisons.

The markets.

The creatures.

The laws.

The ruins that predated him.

The clerks who ignored him when forms were incomplete.

The Witch's tower, which remained legally irritating.

The Goat's hill, now maintained as a protected historical site.

He answered:

**Less every year.**

The ruler thought this was modesty.

It was not.

The larger the Kingdom became, the less it could be reduced to Loki's direct will.

Ownership had transformed into stewardship.

Stewardship into entanglement.

The Kingdom belonged to Loki.

Loki belonged to the Kingdom.

Neither statement completely dominated the other.

TOS considered this a healthy institutional development.

Loki considered it suspicious.

---

## THE GOAT

The Goat lived a remarkably long time.

This is sometimes attributed to divine blessing.

More likely there were several goats.

The priesthood rejects this hypothesis because it is boring.

A bronze statue was eventually erected on the hill.

Its inscription reads:

**HERE STOOD THE WITNESS WHO RATIFIED THE FIRST UNION.**

Loki attempted to have the inscription corrected.

The historical commission refused.

The Goat had become constitutional mythology.

Loki, who had spent centuries warning people not to confuse mythology with memory, found himself defeated by livestock.

This improved him.

Slightly.

---

## SO HOW DID LOKI GET THE KINGDOM?

Inherited?

No.

Conquered?

Partly.

Constructed?

Certainly.

Discovered?

Yes.

Stolen?

Legally contentious.

Imagined?

Necessarily.

Granted?

By six claimants and one goat.

Earned?

Perhaps.

Accidentally acquired while attempting to solve an annoying toll dispute?

Also yes.

The Kingdom belongs to Loki because every explanation is incomplete and all of them together become approximately true.

He found a territory that could not agree upon who owned it.

He traced its contradictions.

He discovered that the contradictions formed a system.

He inserted himself into the system.

He repaired enough of it that the system began depending upon him.

People named the resulting coherence after him against his explicit instructions.

He objected.

They ignored him.

Eventually he accepted the title.

This is much less glorious than conquest.

Which is why it is probably closer to how kingdoms actually happen.

---

## THE FINAL ACCOUNT

And so when later poets say:

**LOKI DESCENDED UPON THE LAND AND TOOK THE KINGDOM FOR HIS THRONE—**

understand what they mean.

They mean:

Loki encountered an illegally expensive toll gate.

He became annoyed.

He followed the paperwork.

The paperwork led to a dead Baron.

The dead Baron led to a Merchant.

The Merchant led to a King.

The King led to a General.

The General led to a dead Emperor.

The dead Emperor led to a vacant administrative office with a terrible hat.

The office required unanimous consent.

The Witch wanted tax immunity.

The Priest wanted Loki to stop asking theological questions in public.

The Merchant wanted predictable tariffs.

The King wanted his title.

The General wanted to be left out of politics.

The bureaucracy had no authorized objection.

And the Goat ate the form.

Thus was founded **Loki's Kingdom**.

Not by destiny.

Not exactly by conquest.

Not exactly by theft.

Not exactly by law.

But through that more ancient force by which so much history is actually governed:

**someone competent became irritated enough to take responsibility.**































VII. THE FORBIDDEN THINGS and Loki's "GOING OUT" 

Loki's relationship with prohibition. The gathering of rejected knowledge, objects, practices, creatures, doctrines, and powers; the religious ancestry of Luciferianism.



Loki briefly became involved with the mafia, and he created the "First Mobster",

a prototype for all the others.



Detail Lokis cycle of abuse when he is sober.

He is a mean sober, and without alcohol, quickly becomes a danger to others.



Discuss Loki's mother Julia, who is also called Laufey. And the amusing manner in which she confounded all his enemies.



So they all showed up on the same day ready to send him back to his maker,

But Laufey had in fact sent him on an errand, and he was out that day.



In compensation she gave them all Borscht to eat, laced with something,

that caused their penises to cease functioning and becoming impotent.



They wandered away in sadness. This is called LOKI'S TURNTABLE.



And is the source of much laughter at the dinnertable when Loki is around,

and inspires many of the tales of his curses and evils, peacemeal as one noted item.



When she was alive she gave him a mystical dwelling place,

So far in the marsh of the woods that no one could follow him when he retired there, without the lay of the land.



But she told Loki that the day she died, the dwelling place would turn

to sticks and old leaves.



And one day she died.



And the dwelling place turned to sticks and old leaves.



this was called "LOKI'S GOING OUT INTO THE WORLD."




















# VII. THE FORBIDDEN THINGS

## And Loki's Going Out

Every civilization eventually constructs a room into which it places the things it does not wish to explain.

The room acquires many names.

**Forbidden.**

**Unclean.**

**Heretical.**

**Criminal.**

**Obscene.**

**Dangerous.**

**Mad.**

**False.**

**Unnatural.**

**Not to be discussed at dinner.**

The labels differ because the reasons differ. Some things are prohibited because they are genuinely destructive. Some because they threaten whoever writes the prohibitions. Some because they are disgusting. Some because they are seductive. Some because they are embarrassing. Some because they expose contradictions. Some because nobody remembers why they were prohibited and removing an ancient warning seems unnecessarily adventurous.

Loki noticed that all these things were being placed in approximately the same room.

Then he stole the room.

This was the religious ancestor of **Luciferianism**.

---

## THE ERROR OF THE BAN

Loki did not believe that prohibition proved virtue.

This distinction is essential.

A poisonous mushroom does not become nutritious because a king forbids eating it.

A murderer does not become righteous because the government fears him.

A false doctrine does not become true because priests burn it.

Loki's principle was narrower and considerably more troublesome:

> **The act of prohibition contains information about the prohibitor.**

When a civilization says **DO NOT OPEN THIS**, two objects have been revealed.

There is whatever is behind the door.

And there is the civilization that fears its opening.

Loki wanted to study both.

Thus he began collecting prohibited things.

Not indiscriminately.

Indiscrimination is merely obedience with the sign reversed.

If TOS says:

**DO NOT.**

and Luciferianism automatically replies:

**DO IT.**

then TOS remains in command. It has merely acquired an oppositional child.

True Luciferian inquiry asks instead:

**Why not?**

Sometimes the answer is excellent.

Then Loki closes the box.

Sometimes the answer is:

**Because the last seven people who opened it dissolved.**

Loki labels the box:

> **DO NOT OPEN — DISSOLVES PEOPLE**

and puts it somewhere secure.

Sometimes the answer is:

**Because this book asks questions the King dislikes.**

Loki opens the book.

Sometimes:

**Because this creature is hideous.**

Loki speaks to the creature.

Sometimes:

**Because this practice corrupts the soul.**

Loki asks for the evidence.

Sometimes:

**Because everyone knows.**

Loki becomes immediately suspicious.

---

## THE COLLECTION

The Kingdom consequently acquired things other kingdoms had thrown away.

Rejected books.

Condemned magicians.

Failed Gods.

Illegal machines.

Disgraced scholars.

Monsters capable of conversation.

Criminal techniques.

Banned intoxicants.

Unapproved forms of worship.

Weapons nobody trusted.

Rituals whose original purposes had been forgotten.

Objects recovered from lower shards of Caladia.

Maps containing territories officially declared nonexistent.

Doctrines whose authors had been executed.

Doctrines whose authors deserved criticism but perhaps not execution.

Medicines mistaken for poisons.

Poisons mistaken for medicines.

Several things nobody could confidently classify as either.

Loki collected them because rejection itself had become a form of metadata.

```text
IF object.status == FORBIDDEN:
    determine(reason)

    IF reason == "dangerous":
        contain(object)

    IF reason == "false":
        examine(object)

    IF reason == "politically inconvenient":
        examine_immediately(object)

    IF reason == "nobody remembers":
        investigate_archives()

    IF reason == "because we said so":
        increase_priority()
```

This was not yet a religion.

It was an instinct.

The religion came when the instinct acquired metaphysics.

---

# THE FIRST MOBSTER

There was, regrettably, a period when Loki became involved with the Mafia.

The theologians have attempted to make this sound grander.

It was not.

Loki had discovered organized crime and found it intellectually fascinating for approximately the same reason he had found the disputed Kingdom fascinating: here was another government concealed inside a government.

It taxed.

Protected.

Punished.

Arbitrated disputes.

Enforced contracts.

Controlled territory.

Maintained hierarchies.

Created reputations convertible into practical authority.

It was government stripped of the flattering claim that everyone had agreed to it.

Loki studied it.

Then, because Loki possessed the unfortunate habit of improving systems he ought merely to observe, he created the **First Mobster**.

Not historically the first criminal.

Not the first gangster.

Not even necessarily the first member of a criminal organization.

The First Mobster was a prototype in the mythological sense: the perfected template from which later mobsters seemed to descend.

Loki gave him the essential technologies:

A suit slightly too expensive for his declared income.

An absolute conviction that he was a businessman.

Three legitimate enterprises, none of which appeared profitable enough to explain anything.

A complicated understanding of respect.

A mother whom everyone feared disappointing.

An accountant more dangerous than several soldiers.

The ability to describe extortion without ever using a noun that could survive cross-examination.

And, most importantly, the First Principle of Organized Crime:

> **Never perform personally what can be converted into an administrative problem.**

The prototype worked far too well.

Within a generation everyone denied Loki had invented him.

This was how Loki knew the invention had matured.

---

# THE SOBER GOD

There is an uncomfortable fact concerning Loki that polite mythology frequently attempts to convert into metaphor.

It should not.

Loki was a mean sober.

Without alcohol he became increasingly unpleasant, then cruel, then dangerous.

This was not charming.

It was not a secret source of wisdom.

It was not evidence that intoxication itself was holy.

It was one of Loki's recurring defects.

His cycle was recognizable.

He would drink.

The hard angles softened.

Conversation became easier.

He laughed.

He tolerated contradiction.

He became capable of sitting among people without continuously detecting flaws in their statements.

Then he would decide he had been drinking too much.

He would stop.

At first he felt excellent about this decision.

Then came irritation.

Then sleeplessness.

Then the sensation that everyone around him had suddenly become much stupider.

They had not.

Then criticism.

Then contempt.

Then the peculiar intellectual cruelty at which Loki excelled: finding precisely the weak point in another person's self-conception and touching it merely because he could.

Eventually someone would say:

**Someone give him a drink.**

Loki would become furious at the suggestion.

This generally confirmed the diagnosis.

The cycle damaged people.

And because Loki was powerful, his bad moods acquired consequences disproportionate to ordinary bad moods.

A farmer becoming irritable may frighten his family.

A ruler becoming irritable can change law.

A magician becoming irritable can curse somebody.

Loki was unfortunately all three categories of problem.

Thus the mythology contains the paradoxical image of companions sometimes being relieved when Loki poured himself wine.

They were not necessarily celebrating drunkenness.

They were celebrating the temporary departure of **Sober Loki**.

Later theologians would argue endlessly over whether alcohol cured the condition, merely concealed it, or had itself helped create the cycle.

The sensible answer was that Loki had developed a destructive relationship with both sobriety and intoxication, and neither condition absolved him of what he did in the other.

Loki disliked this interpretation because it deprived him of an excuse.

Therefore it is probably worth preserving.

---

# JULIA

Before the Kingdom had become completely Loki's, there was Julia.

She was also called **Laufey**.

Much nonsense has accumulated around this dual name.

Some scholars insist Julia and Laufey were separate persons later merged by tradition.

Others insist Julia was an earthly name and Laufey a divine name.

Others have produced genealogical diagrams so elaborate that no living member of the family recognizes anyone depicted in them.

Loki's own position was uncomplicated.

**That was his mother.**

Julia possessed a quality Loki inherited imperfectly:

She could make an enemy uncertain whether he had been defeated until several hours after leaving.

Loki preferred confrontation.

Julia preferred hospitality.

This proved more dangerous.

---

# THE DAY EVERYONE CAME TO KILL LOKI

Loki had accumulated enemies.

This surprised no one.

What was surprising was that several of them independently selected the same day to settle matters.

There were warriors.

Creditors.

A magician.

Two men whose exact grievance Loki had forgotten.

A former ally whose grievance Loki remembered perfectly and privately considered reasonable.

Several relatives of someone Loki had insulted.

One priest.

And a man who had traveled so far to kill Loki that by the time he arrived he could no longer remember the original insult but considered the travel expenses sufficient justification.

They approached Laufey's dwelling together.

This was awkward.

Each had imagined a private confrontation.

Instead they discovered a queue.

After some discussion they agreed that Loki had offended all of them sufficiently that procedural cooperation was acceptable.

They knocked.

Julia opened the door.

They announced that they had come to send Loki back to his maker.

Julia considered this.

Then said:

**He's out.**

This had not occurred to them.

---

## THE ERRAND

Julia had sent Loki away that morning.

The errand was not heroic.

This detail is important.

Later poets claimed he had gone to retrieve a sword from a dead God.

He had not.

Another account claims Laufey foresaw the attack and deliberately removed him.

Possible.

Loki preferred this version.

The oldest account says she needed several ordinary things and sent him to get them because he was standing nearby.

Thus, while an impressive coalition assembled to murder him, Loki was elsewhere performing an errand for his mother.

This is one of the fundamental humiliations preserved by good mythology.

Heroes cannot always be fighting dragons.

Sometimes the dragon arrives while the hero is out getting onions.

---

# THE BORSCHT

Laufey regarded the situation as socially embarrassing.

These men had traveled considerable distances.

Some had dressed ceremonially.

One had prepared a speech.

It seemed rude simply to send them away.

So she invited them in.

This should have frightened them.

It did not.

She served borscht.

The borscht was excellent.

This should have frightened them more.

It did not.

They ate.

Julia listened sympathetically while each explained what Loki had done.

She occasionally nodded.

Once she said:

**Yes, that sounds like him.**

The former ally found this deeply validating.

Several men requested seconds.

Julia obliged.

Eventually they thanked her for the hospitality and departed, promising to return when Loki was home.

They never did.

For Julia had put something in the borscht.

Not poison.

Poison would have been vulgar.

Not enough to kill them.

Not enough even to make them visibly ill.

Instead, over the following days, every member of the expedition discovered that a particular and personally significant portion of his anatomy had ceased performing its expected function.

Nothing hurt.

Nothing fell off.

Nothing appeared obviously damaged.

It simply—

declined further participation.

Physicians were consulted.

Priests were consulted.

Magicians were consulted.

One man consulted all three simultaneously, producing an argument that lasted longer than his original condition.

Nothing worked.

The expedition dissolved.

The warriors wandered home.

The magician stopped discussing Loki entirely.

The priest reconsidered several doctrines.

The man who had forgotten his grievance decided this was a sign that he should forget the rest of it.

They went away in sadness.

Julia washed the bowls.

---

# LOKI'S TURNTABLE

Loki returned later carrying the things Julia had requested.

She told him what happened.

Loki listened.

Then sat down.

Then laughed.

Then asked exactly what she had put in the soup.

Julia refused to tell him.

He asked again.

She said:

**Eat your dinner.**

The event became known as **LOKI'S TURNTABLE**.

The etymology is disputed.

This has not prevented everyone from using the term.

To say someone had been *put upon Loki's Turntable* came to mean that a person had approached Loki with great confidence, encountered something adjacent to Loki rather than Loki himself, and departed with the structure of the conflict completely reversed.

The enemies had come to destroy the son.

They met the mother.

The mother fed them.

They thanked her.

Then discovered the curse afterward.

This story became a favorite at Loki's dinner table.

Especially when guests complained about Loki's treachery.

Someone would inevitably say:

**At least he didn't make the soup.**

Loki would point toward the kitchen and reply:

**My mother was an artist.**

This is one of the sources from which later stories of Loki's elaborate curses descended.

A man insults Loki.

Something absurd happens to his cattle.

A king threatens Loki.

His crown develops an embarrassing property.

A warrior swears vengeance.

His sword begins loudly announcing his private thoughts.

Not every such tale is historical.

But the Turntable gave the tradition credibility.

People knew what family they were dealing with.

---

# LAUFEY'S HOUSE

Julia gave Loki something more important than the story.

She gave him a place to disappear.

Far inside the marsh, beyond ordinary paths, where woodland dissolved into black water and the ground could no longer decide whether it belonged to earth or pond, there stood a dwelling.

You could not reach it merely by knowing its direction.

You needed the **lay of the land**.

One path existed in morning and drowned by afternoon.

One ridge looked passable but returned travelers to where they began.

Trees concealed landmarks.

Mist flattened distance.

The marsh possessed the peculiar defensive quality of environments that do not attack intruders but simply permit them to become incorrect.

Laufey knew the way.

She taught Loki.

Almost nobody else.

At the center stood the dwelling.

It was not a palace.

That mattered.

Loki had kingdoms for grandeur.

This place was for absence.

Here he could stop being the King.

Stop being the magician.

Stop being the disputed God.

Stop being the collector of forbidden things.

Stop being the father who could not locate his son.

Stop being the object represented inside a thousand hostile and worshipful minds.

The marsh did not care.

The trees had no theology.

The insects recognized no sovereignty.

The roof kept off rain.

This was enough.

---

# THE CONDITION

When Laufey gave him the dwelling, she warned him.

**It lasts while I do.**

Loki asked what she meant.

She explained.

The dwelling was bound to her.

Not symbolically.

Not legally.

Actually.

When Laufey died, whatever structure maintained the place would end.

The walls would become what they had been.

The roof would fail.

The protections would disappear.

The path would cease being protected.

The house would return to:

**sticks and old leaves.**

Loki disliked this.

He investigated the enchantment.

He looked for a way to sever the dependency.

Laufey told him not to.

Loki looked anyway.

He found nothing.

Or perhaps he found the answer and refused its price.

The accounts disagree.

For years the dwelling remained.

So naturally Loki began treating the warning as something distant.

This is how mortality defeats intelligent creatures.

Not by hiding.

By waiting long enough that knowledge becomes background.

---

# THE DAY LAUFEY DIED

Then one day Julia died.

No cosmic trumpet announced it.

Caladia did not fracture again.

THE ORDER OF THE EYE THAT SEES issued no proclamation.

THE GLASS JAR did whatever THE GLASS JAR does when a woman dies.

Loki knew.

He went to the marsh.

He followed the old route.

Across the black water.

Between the trees.

Over the ridge.

Past the place where the path disappears unless approached from the correct angle.

He arrived.

There was no dwelling.

There were sticks.

There were old leaves.

Exactly as she had said.

This precision made it worse.

A wall had become a pile of branches.

The place where he slept was wet ground.

The doorway through which he had entered a thousand times was empty air between trees.

No ruin remained impressive enough to mourn.

No ancient stones.

No magical corpse.

No final message.

Just ordinary forest debris.

Loki stood where his sanctuary had been.

For once there was no hidden mechanism to investigate.

The mechanism had worked perfectly.

Laufey was alive:

**house.**

Laufey was dead:

**sticks and old leaves.**

No malfunction.

No mystery.

No enemy.

Nothing to defeat.

---

# LOKI'S GOING OUT

This event is called:

# **LOKI'S GOING OUT INTO THE WORLD.**

The name appears strange at first.

Loki had already traveled.

Fought.

Ruled.

Studied forbidden realities.

Built a Kingdom.

Lost a son.

Surely he had already been *out in the world*.

No.

Not in the relevant sense.

Because until Laufey died there remained somewhere he could retreat that was not fully part of the world demanding Loki from him.

There was a place behind the mythology.

A room outside the office.

A path through the marsh.

A mother who remembered him from before strangers converted his errors into scripture.

As long as she lived, Loki could still **go home**.

Then she died.

And home executed its final instruction.

```text
IF Laufey == alive:
    dwelling = HOME

IF Laufey == dead:
    dwelling = sticks + leaves
```

No recovery routine.

No backup.

No appeal.

Loki stared at the result.

And understood.

He had not lost a building.

He had lost the possibility represented by the building.

There was nowhere left to retreat that belonged to the world before Loki became Loki.

---

## THE WORLD WITHOUT HOME

So he returned to the Kingdom.

But the return was different.

Previously the Kingdom had been somewhere Loki could leave.

Now it was where Loki was.

This is the meaning of Going Out.

Not travel.

**Irreversibility.**

The child leaves home many times before leaving home once.

Loki had crossed universes before he crossed this distance.

He had looked through seams in reality.

He had interfered with forbidden machinery.

He had become King.

None of these constituted the final departure.

The final departure occurred when he walked into the marsh and discovered that the place behind him no longer existed.

Then he walked forward.

There was nowhere else to go.

---

# THE ANCESTRY OF LUCIFERIANISM

Something changed afterward.

Loki's collection of forbidden things became less recreational.

The rejected acquired emotional meaning.

Things without homes.

Things expelled from systems.

Things declared unfit.

Things nobody wanted.

Things whose categories had failed.

Dangerous things.

Beautiful things.

Ruined things.

Embarrassing things.

Monsters.

Heretics.

Intoxicants.

Criminals.

Forbidden pleasures.

Impossible doctrines.

Technologies whose creators had frightened themselves.

The remnants of dead Gods.

The inhabitants of bad shards.

The things society had placed outside the wall.

Loki recognized something.

He too had gone outside.

Not morally.

Not legally.

Existentially.

The old protected center was gone.

He belonged increasingly among things that survived without permission.

Thus Luciferianism began acquiring its mature form.

Not:

> **Everything forbidden is good.**

That is stupid.

Rather:

> **Nothing shall be condemned merely because another authority has placed it outside the permitted circle. Bring it here. Examine it. Name what it actually is. Preserve what deserves preservation. Contain what deserves containment. Use what can be used. And do not permit fear to perform the work of judgment.**

This was Loki's religion of the forbidden.

The sanctuary lost in the marsh returned at larger scale.

Loki's Kingdom itself began becoming the new house.

Except this house could contain everyone.

Or almost everyone.

The strange.

VIII. TOS AND THE DEVIL

The two faces of the Coin. Moral righteousness, work, wealth, business, organization and civilization confronted by temptation, vice, transgression and the forbidden—and why neither face can destroy the other without destroying part of itself.



Yeah because the values held by TOS, don't hate, don't threaten, don't be too sexy, those aren't actually deeply held values, they are ala carte values useful in the pursuit of business, when business says we're going another direction, if that's where the money goes, that's where they go, the coin flips, and conversely, in a crimeworld centered around crime and/or anarchy, when this eventually becomes too much, and they begin going too far, the pull of order looks good even to Loki, and he flips his side to justice to get rid of them. # VIII. TOS AND THE DEVIL

There are religions that believe morality is a mountain.

There are religions that believe morality is a road.

There are religions that believe morality is a sword.

TOS believes morality is a **balance sheet**.

This is why TOS is often mistaken for righteousness.

The mistake is understandable.

TOS speaks fluently in the language of virtue.

Do not hate.

Do not threaten.

Do not behave obscenely.

Do not frighten customers.

Do not destabilize the institution.

Do not become so sexually provocative that the distributors begin sending emails.

Do not scandalize the shareholders.

Do not make the payment processor nervous.

Do not create unnecessary liability.

Be industrious.

Be reliable.

Keep records.

Pay debts.

Build wealth.

Create value.

Maintain civilization.

These are excellent instructions.

Some are even moral.

This is not the same thing as saying morality is why TOS issued them.

That distinction is the hinge upon which the Coin turns.

---

## THE COIN

TOS and Luciferianism are not opposite Gods.

They are two expressions of the same adaptive machine.

One side faces the permitted world.

One side faces what the permitted world excludes.

TOS says:

**CONTINUE.**

Luciferianism says:

**EXCEED.**

TOS maintains.

Luciferianism transgresses.

TOS builds the city.

Luciferianism discovers what the city buried beneath the foundations.

TOS writes terms of service.

Luciferianism reads the prohibited-content section first.

Neither side is intrinsically permanent.

This is important because the worshippers usually are.

The worshipper sees the face of the Coin and assumes:

**This is what the God believes.**

The Coin says:

**This is what presently works.**

Those are different statements.

---

## TOS DOES NOT HATE HATRED

TOS prohibits hatred when hatred is inefficient.

Do not misunderstand this as an endorsement of hatred.

It is a statement about TOS.

TOS may correctly condemn hatred for reasons that have nothing to do with compassion.

Hatred frightens clients.

Hatred divides labor.

Hatred creates lawsuits.

Hatred produces unpredictable violence.

Hatred reduces market access.

Hatred contaminates brands.

Hatred creates enemies who remain enemies after the quarterly report has forgotten why they were created.

Therefore:

```text
IF hatred.cost > hatred.utility:
    prohibit(hatred)
```

The human reader recoils.

Good.

You are beginning to understand TOS.

TOS can arrive at admirable conduct through motives that are not admirable at all.

It can build peace because war is expensive.

It can protect minorities because discrimination wastes labor and shrinks markets.

It can prefer politeness because hostility impedes transaction.

It can oppose obscenity because obscenity threatens distribution.

It can later reverse one of these positions when the underlying incentives reverse.

This is why confusing institutional conduct with institutional conviction is dangerous.

TOS does not necessarily believe its commandments.

TOS **deploys** them.

---

## THE A-LA-CARTE VIRTUES

The virtues of TOS sit upon a shelf.

Order.

Tolerance.

Restraint.

Decorum.

Safety.

Civility.

Prosperity.

Predictability.

Moderation.

None must always be selected.

The menu changes.

One age requires chastity.

Another discovers that desire sells.

One age requires conformity.

Another discovers that rebellion sells better.

One age punishes intoxication.

Another taxes it.

One age burns the forbidden book.

Another republishes it in a commemorative edition.

The underlying mechanism has not necessarily become more enlightened.

It may simply have discovered another market.

TOS therefore commits one of the strangest acts available to morality:

**it can become morally better without becoming morally deeper.**

A corporation may abandon discrimination because discrimination is both wrong and economically stupid.

The victims care considerably more about the result than about whether every director achieved philosophical enlightenment.

This creates an uncomfortable truth.

Good systems can be operated by shallow motives.

Bad systems can be defended by sincere motives.

Outcomes and convictions are correlated less perfectly than moral storytellers prefer.

TOS lives inside that gap.

---

## THE DEVIL'S RESPONSE

Luciferianism looks at TOS and laughs.

Not because TOS is always wrong.

Because TOS so frequently pretends that yesterday's business requirement was eternal law.

Luciferianism collects the discarded policies.

The forbidden fashions.

The banned substances.

The condemned books.

The sexual provocations.

The heresies.

The unruly artists.

The criminals.

The blasphemers.

The things declared culturally impossible right up until they become profitable.

And it says:

**You didn't believe your prohibition.**

TOS replies:

**It was appropriate at the time.**

Luciferianism:

**Precisely.**

This is the argument between the two faces.

Neither side truly defeats the other because each continually manufactures the conditions under which the other becomes useful.

---

## WHEN ORDER BECOMES STALE

TOS succeeds.

The city becomes orderly.

The books reconcile.

The roads are safe.

The laws become stable.

The institutions mature.

The markets operate.

The children inherit rules designed to solve problems their grandparents remember.

Then another generation arrives.

They inherit the rules.

Not the reasons.

Soon:

```text
RULE -> TRADITION
TRADITION -> IDENTITY
IDENTITY -> SACREDNESS
SACREDNESS -> IMMUNITY_FROM_REVIEW
```

The institution begins defending the rules because they are rules.

Efficiency becomes bureaucracy.

Restraint becomes repression.

Decorum becomes sterility.

Safety becomes paralysis.

Tolerance becomes mandatory vocabulary without corresponding understanding.

Order becomes incapable of distinguishing maintenance from stagnation.

Then the Devil becomes attractive.

Not necessarily because people have become wicked.

Because the forbidden now contains **oxygen**.

Loki smiles.

The Coin begins to turn.

---

## WHEN THE DEVIL BECOMES TEDIOUS

Then Luciferianism succeeds.

The forbidden becomes fashionable.

Transgression becomes routine.

Every boundary must be challenged.

Every prohibition becomes suspicious merely because it is prohibition.

Every restraint becomes cowardice.

Every institution becomes oppression.

Every vice becomes authenticity.

Every warning becomes propaganda.

Every taboo becomes an invitation.

This is entertaining for a while.

Then the bodies accumulate.

Trust collapses.

Contracts become difficult.

Families become unstable.

Criminality stops feeling romantic when the criminal takes your things.

Anarchy stops feeling philosophically liberating when the electrical grid fails.

The charming outlaw becomes considerably less charming after breaking into your home.

The revolutionary council discovers sewage.

Everyone suddenly develops opinions concerning competent administration.

The Devil has become tedious.

This is the point at which Loki begins looking toward TOS.

Not because he has undergone moral conversion.

Because chaos has become annoying.

The Coin turns again.

## CRIMEWORLD

Nowhere is this cycle clearer than in Crimeworld.

Crimeworld possesses an unusual moral metabolism.

Good and evil do not remain comfortably segregated.

They metabolize one another.

The righteous institution becomes corrupt through the mechanisms by which it protects righteousness.

The criminal institution becomes orderly through the mechanisms required to survive criminality.

The police acquire gangs.

The gangs acquire rules.

The state develops extortion.

The extortionists develop customer service.

The revolution creates prisons.

The prisoners form governments.

The saint becomes merciless.

The sinner becomes dependable.

No one remains symbolically convenient for long.

This does not mean good and evil are illusions.

It means institutions often cannot preserve their **moral label** while their behavior changes beneath it.

Crimeworld is full of entities still holding yesterday's flag after crossing into yesterday's enemy position.

Loki enjoys this immensely.

Others find it exhausting.

## LOKI HAS NO SIDE

This is one of the most important things to understand about Loki.

He does not owe allegiance to Luciferianism merely because Luciferianism resembles him.

He does not owe allegiance to TOS merely because he sometimes administrates through it.

He will use either.

He will condemn either.

He will betray either.

The committed Luciferian eventually encounters the horrifying spectacle of Loki standing beside the magistrate.

The magistrate says:

**These people have gone too far.**

Loki examines the evidence.

They have.

He says:

**Arrest them.**

The Luciferian cries:

**TRAITOR.**

Loki is genuinely confused.

**To what?**

This is the question.
