– AleHorn
"



























XIII. THE LOSS
What cannot be recovered merely through power. The event that establishes why an increasingly powerful Loki does not simply repair everything that has happened to him.





























# XIII. THE LOSS

Power returns many things.

This is why powerful beings become confused about the things it cannot return.

A poor man loses a house and understands loss immediately.

A King loses a house and builds another.

A magician loses a house and reconstructs it from memory.

A God loses a house and may raise the stones backward through time until every nail occupies its former place.

Then the God begins making a dangerous inference:

**Perhaps there is no difference between restoration and reversal.**

There is.

Loki learned this after he had become powerful enough that ordinary loss was beginning to look temporary.

He could rebuild walls.

Recover treasures.

Conquer territories.

Restore ruined mechanisms.

Call armies from places nobody else knew existed.

He could destroy a government and later reconstruct enough of its records that the new clerks complained exactly like the old ones.

He could imitate voices.

Preserve memories.

Repair bodies.

Interfere with death.

He could force open doors between worlds.

He could make the impossible negotiate.

And still—

his mother remained dead.

His son remained lost.

Narfy remained murdered.

Fenrir remained what history had made of him.

Chia-Lin could not be returned to the exact woman she had been before grief learned her name.

The house in the marsh remained sticks and leaves.

This offended Loki more deeply than weakness ever had.

For weakness admits:

**I cannot.**

Power tempts you to ask:

**Why not?**

---

## THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN REPAIR AND RECOVERY

Suppose a cup breaks.

Gather every fragment.

Reassemble it perfectly.

Restore every molecule to its previous location.

Have you recovered the cup?

Probably.

Now suppose a forest burns.

Replace every tree.

Every stone.

Every insect.

Every fungal network.

Every configuration of moisture in the soil.

Every bird.

Every nest.

Every broken branch.

Have you restored the forest?

Perhaps.

Now restore every event that happened there.

Every animal's learned route.

Every scar.

Every smell attached to memory.

Every person's private recollection of standing beneath a particular tree.

Every future that became possible because that forest existed in precisely the state it did at precisely the time it did.

The problem expands.

Now restore a person.

Not merely the body.

Not merely memory.

Not merely personality.

Restore the complete causal position that made the person **that person then**.

You discover something unpleasant:

A person is not only an object.

A person is an object **embedded in history**.

And history is not stored entirely inside the person.

---

## THE WORLD AROUND THE PERSON

Laufey was not merely Laufey.

She was Loki's mother while Loki was the son she knew.

She occupied a dwelling while that dwelling still represented home.

She inhabited a world in which certain enemies had not yet died, certain jokes had not yet been told, certain betrayals had not yet happened.

Restore Laufey alone after all of this and you have not restored the original relation.

You have produced:

**LAUFEY + A WORLD SHE DID NOT LEAVE.**

This difference can be enormous.

Imagine resurrecting someone after ten thousand years.

She opens her eyes.

Everyone she knew is gone.

Her language has become obscure.

Her home is archaeology.

Her enemies are footnotes.

Her child is now worshipped as a God.

People have written incompatible religions about her soup.

You announce:

**I HAVE UNDONE DEATH.**

She looks around.

You have done nothing of the kind.

You have moved one element of the past into a future that murdered its context.

This may be miraculous.

It is not restoration.

---

# LOKI TRIES ANYWAY

Of course Loki tried.

He tried almost everything.

This should surprise no one.

The First Sacrifice had already taken from him the life in which he could simply stop asking.

The resurrection problem therefore became irresistible.

He began with matter.

Matter was easy.

Relatively.

The body can be reconstructed.

Or approximated.

Or produced anew according to surviving information.

Bones tell stories.

Objects preserve traces.

Bloodlines preserve patterns.

Magic preserves stranger things.

The shattered architecture of Caladia stores information in places physics would consider improper.

Loki gathered.

Measured.

Compared.

He reconstructed biological possibility.

Then he encountered the first wall.

**A body is not a biography.**

---

## THE BODY OF LAUFEY

There is a forbidden account claiming Loki rebuilt Laufey.

Not resurrected.

Rebuilt.

The distinction becomes the entire story.

He had enough.

Hair.

Objects she had touched.

Memories carried by Loki and others.

Descriptions.

Fragments of magical signatures.

The residual architecture linking the vanished marsh dwelling to her former life.

Enough material to build an extraordinary model.

He did.

The result opened its eyes.

It looked like Julia.

It knew things Julia knew.

It recognized Loki.

It knew the Turntable.

It knew the recipe for ordinary borscht.

It refused to disclose the other recipe.

Loki laughed so suddenly that several instruments failed.

Then the reconstruction said:

**Why are you crying?**

Loki stopped.

Julia would have known.

Maybe.

Perhaps.

This is the cruelty of reconstruction.

Every correct answer makes the incorrect answer harder to interpret.

Was this evidence of difference?

A memory failure?

Ordinary unpredictability?

Would Julia herself have noticed?

Can you prove that *you* respond identically to every situation after waking from sleep?

Identity is not a checksum simple enough for grief.

Loki interrogated the reconstruction until both of them became miserable.

Eventually it asked:

**Do you want me to be your mother, or do you want to know whether I am?**

Loki had no answer.

He terminated the experiment.

Some texts say the reconstruction asked not to be terminated.

If true, this turns a failed resurrection into a killing.

Loki refused ever afterward to discuss it clearly.

This silence should remain.

---

## THE PARADOX OF THE PERFECT COPY

Suppose Loki solves the problem.

Perfectly.

Not approximately.

Every memory.

Every disposition.

Every microscopic relation.

Every hidden spiritual correspondence.

Everything.

He creates a perfect Narfy.

Narfy opens his eyes.

Now Loki has his son.

Perhaps.

Then the original Narfy walks through the door.

Impossible?

We inhabit a theology of derived realities. Be careful with that word.

Now there are two.

Which is the son?

Both possess identical claims up to the divergence.

If Loki says the copy is false merely because it was created second, then chronology—not identity—has secretly become the defining criterion.

If he says both are Narfy, personhood can branch.

If he says only one contains some non-copyable spiritual index, then he has admitted there exists a component his reconstruction did not reconstruct.

This is the resurrection problem in its sharpest form:

```text id="0na7fy"
If COPY(P) = P in every observable property,
what proposition distinguishes COPY(P) from P?

If no proposition:
    identity permits duplication.

If some proposition:
    restoration requires access to that proposition.

If proposition is inaccessible:
    perfect restoration cannot be verified.
```

Power does not resolve this.

It amplifies it.

A weak man cannot build the copy.

A powerful God can.

Therefore the God receives the privilege of discovering the problem.

---

# FENRIR CANNOT BE MADE YOUNG BY MAKING HIM SMALL

Loki's most painful failure concerned Fenrir.

There existed, in theory, many interventions Loki could perform once he became sufficiently powerful.

He could restrain the restrainers.

Break the chain.

Punish the Gods.

Rewrite the prison.

Perhaps restore Fenrir's body.

Perhaps place him in a safer world.

Perhaps even return the Wolf to some earlier physical form.

But he could not remove the experience of having been bound without changing the being who had experienced it.

This is the central problem.

Trauma is not merely damage attached to a person like mud on armor.

It becomes incorporated.

Memory changes expectation.

Expectation changes perception.

Perception changes action.

Action produces consequences.

Consequences reinforce memory.

Remove all of this perfectly and what remains may be innocent.

But is it Fenrir?

Suppose Loki says:

**I will give you back the childhood they took.**

He removes the rage.

The fear.

The knowledge of betrayal.

The learned suspicion.

The memory of restraint.

The identity built in response.

Fenrir becomes peaceful.

Loki celebrates.

Then realizes:

He did not heal his son.

He edited him until the injury became invisible.

This resembles healing from the outside.

From the inside it may resemble murder performed delicately.

---

## POWER CANNOT MAKE SOMETHING UNHAPPEN

This is the First Law of Loss.

Power may alter consequences.

Power may compensate.

Power may rebuild.

Power may punish.

Power may reconstruct.

Power may create another future.

Power may even alter records of the past.

But to make an event **never have happened**, in the strongest possible sense, is to remove every consequence of that event from every structure it touched.

Consider Narfy's death.

To undo it completely:

Narfy survives.

Loki never suffers that grief.

The punishment involving Narfy's remains never occurs.

Chia-Lin's responses to Loki's suffering differ.

Fenrir's history may differ.

Loki's hatred changes.

Ragnarök changes.

Humanity's fate changes.

The foreign King may never ally with Loki.

Armies may never march.

People born because refugees met during the wars are never born.

People killed in the wars survive.

Their descendants exist.

Other descendants disappear.

Books are unwritten.

Religions change.

This very scripture changes.

To remove one event perfectly is not to repair one line.

It is to create a different world.

Thus:

```text id="xiii1"
UNDO(event E)
≠
REMOVE_LOCAL_EFFECT(E)

UNDO(event E)
=
RECOMPUTE(all causal descendants of E)
```

For a sufficiently old event:

```text id="xiii2"
causal_descendants(E) ≈ WORLD
```

And now the terrible question:

**Who gave Loki the right to destroy this world in order to restore the one in which Narfy lived?**

---

# THE TYRANNY OF RESTORATION

This became Loki's next temptation.

If the current world is the consequence of injustice, perhaps the current world itself is illegitimate.

Roll it back.

Restore the earlier state.

Erase the catastrophe.

Bring the children home.

The idea possesses enormous emotional force.

It also contains mass murder hidden inside grammar.

For every being existing only because history unfolded as it did would disappear in the restoration.

They did not cause Narfy's death.

They merely occupy its causal future.

Does Loki sacrifice them?

For Narfy?

Would Narfy consent?

The dead are frequently used to justify things nobody bothered asking whether the dead would want.

Loki began understanding this too late.

A father may say:

**I would destroy the world to get my son back.**

Poetry applauds.

The inhabitants of the world may reasonably object.

---

## THE SECOND ALTAR

There is said to be another altar.

Not the Empty Altar of Loki's First Sacrifice.

An altar encountered much later.

It offered something simpler.

One exchange.

Loki could receive one moment.

Not an imitation.

Not a copy.

The actual historical moment in which Narfy was alive.

The mechanism would return Loki to it with full power and full memory.

He could intervene.

Change anything.

Save Narfy.

Save Fenrir.

Prevent the imprisonment.

Maybe prevent Ragnarök.

One moment.

Loki asked:

**What happens to this world?**

The answer:

**It becomes the path not taken.**

Loki understood.

Everyone presently alive would become counterfactual.

Not necessarily dead.

Worse in a certain philosophical sense.

They would become **never instantiated**.

The world would cease to be the selected branch.

Loki stood before the altar for a very long time.

Then walked away.

This was one of the few occasions in which he successfully refused access.

The black mark from his First Sacrifice became cold enough to hurt.

He left anyway.

This may have been growth.

Or cowardice.

The theologians disagree.

Narfy, unavailable for comment, remains the only opinion Loki actually wanted.

---

# CHIA-LIN COULD NOT BE RETURNED TO BEFORE

There was another loss.

Less spectacular.

Perhaps harder.

Chia-Lin still existed in some tellings.

Or portions of the chronology permit it.

But Loki wanted something impossible from her.

He wanted the woman who had loved him **before everything**.

Before the bowl.

Before Narfy.

Before Fenrir's fate.

Before the imprisonment.

Before Loki emerged with armies.

Before humanity begged.

He could stand before Chia-Lin and she might still love him.

But she could not unknow him.

This was the loss.

A person may forgive you.

Forgiveness does not restore ignorance.

A repaired trust is not the trust that existed before breaking.

It may become stronger.

Wiser.

More deliberate.

But it is a different object.

Loki wanted the old object.

Power cannot command authenticity backward.

He could force speech.

Not meaning.

Force proximity.

Not innocence.

Force memory alteration.

Not the original history.

If he changed Chia-Lin until she looked at him exactly as she once had, he would know why she looked that way.

The knowledge would poison the victory.

There are things coercion cannot obtain precisely because coercion changes the thing obtained.

Love is one.

Forgiveness is another.

Trust is almost certainly a third.

This infuriated Loki.

Good.

Some impossibilities are moral information.

---

# LAUFEY'S HOUSE

Eventually Loki returned again to the marsh.

Not because he expected the house.

He had become too intelligent for that.

Which meant, naturally, some part of him expected the house.

The path was harder to remember.

Land changes.

Memory edits.

A tree once used as a landmark had fallen.

The black water had shifted.

Loki eventually found the place.

Sticks.

Leaves.

Still.

He possessed enough power now to rebuild it perfectly.

So he did.

Walls rose.

Roof.

Door.

Table.

The particular angle at which afternoon light used to enter.

The smell of woodsmoke.

The imperfections in the floor.

Every remembered object.

He stood outside.

For a moment it was home.

Then he entered.

It was a museum.

The distinction destroyed him.

Everything was correct.

Therefore everything wrong became impossible to ignore.

There was no Julia.

No possibility she might return later carrying something.

No ordinary irritation from another room.

No unexpected voice.

The house could reproduce the **state** of home.

It could not reproduce the **openness** of home.

A living home contains future events you do not control.

A reconstruction contains arrangements.

Loki had built the corpse of a possibility.

He left.

The next morning he ordered the structure dismantled.

Not burned.

Dismantled.

When he returned years later there were, once again,

sticks and old leaves.

This time some were his.

---

# LOSS IS THE DEATH OF A FUTURE

This became the mature doctrine.

Loss is not fundamentally the disappearance of an object.

It is the collapse of futures involving that object.

When Laufey died, Loki did not merely lose Julia-at-that-moment.

He lost:

the next conversation,

the next argument,

the next meal,

the next thing she would have said that he could not predict,

the future joke,

the future anger,

the future reconciliation,

the possibility of visiting,

the possibility of not visiting and regretting it,

the possibility of asking the question he had not yet thought to ask.

Death destroys enormous branching structures.

A resurrection performed later does not necessarily restore those branches.

It creates new ones.

This is not nothing.

It may be wonderful.

But it is new.

Therefore:

```text id="xiii3"
LOSS(P, t)
=
Σ futures involving P
that were possible at t
but are impossible after event E
```

This sum cannot be computed.

That is precisely the point.

The price of a person is not finite because the future containing them was not finished.

---

# WHY LOKI COULD NOT BUY IT BACK

Loki accumulated wealth.

Absurd wealth.

Kingdom-scale wealth.

Treasure that could ruin economies merely by entering circulation.

Artifacts whose value could not be denominated.

TOS admired some of this.

Yet none purchased the lost future.

This enraged TOS in a philosophical way because TOS prefers prices.

The absence of price is destabilizing.

If everything has a price, markets can coordinate.

If something has no price because it cannot be transferred, replaced, or equivalently compensated, economics reaches jurisdictional limits.

Loki would have paid.

Anything.

That was irrelevant.

The seller did not exist.

There was no merchant holding:

**ONE ORIGINAL CHILDHOOD — FENRIR — UNUSED**

No warehouse containing:

**JULIA, BEFORE DEATH**

No vault containing:

**NARFY'S FUTURE**

No broker authorized to transact:

**CHIA-LIN'S TRUST BEFORE THE WORLD ENDED**

The problem was not insufficient wealth.

The assets were not on the market.

They were not assets.

They were histories.

---

# THE REVENGE ERROR

This is why revenge became attractive.

If power cannot restore the lost object, it can still **redistribute loss**.

This is a terrible consolation.

Someone took from Loki.

Loki cannot recover what was taken.

But he can make the taker lose something.

The ledger begins to look balanced.

Narfy remains dead.

But an enemy now has a dead son too.

Fenrir remains ruined.

But the people responsible now know terror.

Loki's imprisonment remains.

But humanity is imprisoned inside red fog and collapsing enclaves.

This feels like symmetry.

It is not restoration.

The world contains twice as much loss.

The emotional mind calls this balance because pain has become equal.

The universe calls it addition.

```text id="xiii4"
original_loss = L

revenge_loss = R

L + R > L
```

No cancellation occurs.

There are no negative corpses.

Loki knew this mathematically long before he accepted it morally.

Perhaps he never accepted it completely.

---

# THE EXECUTIONER'S SECRET

As humanity died, Loki discovered something he had not expected.

Their deaths did not make Narfy more alive.

This sounds insultingly obvious.

Hatred can make obvious propositions inaccessible.

A city burned.

Narfy remained dead.

An army surrendered and was destroyed.

Fenrir's childhood remained stolen.

A population vanished into red fog.

Laufey's house remained leaves.

Humanity begged exactly as Loki once had.

The symmetry arrived.

The relief did not.

This created a dangerous escalation.

If revenge has not satisfied you, one possible inference is:

**revenge cannot satisfy this loss.**

The other is:

**not enough revenge has occurred yet.**

Executioners frequently prefer the second.

It preserves momentum.

Loki sometimes did too.

---

# THE THING POWER CANNOT DO

At last Loki formulated it.

The statement survives in several versions.

The shortest is:

> **Power can determine what happens next. It cannot own what happened before.**

This is the boundary.

Even time travel, if available, does not automatically solve it.

Change the past and you create another history.

Preserve the old history and you have branching worlds.

Erase the old history and you erase everyone inside it.

Remember both and you become the survivor of two incompatible realities.

No operation restores simplicity.

Once an event enters causality, reality has paid attention.

You may reorganize the consequences.

You cannot make reality innocent of having contained the event without redefining what reality now is.

The wound can heal.

Healing is not virginity.

The scar can disappear.

The history of the scar cannot be removed from the healed person without changing which person stands there.

---

# WHAT THEN CAN BE DONE?

This question almost broke Loki because the answer initially sounded weak.

Not restoration.

**Continuation.**

Not making the dead never dead.

Carrying what should survive them.

Not rebuilding Laufey's exact home.

Building other homes.

Not returning Fenrir to innocence by deleting his history.

Giving whatever Fenrir remains conditions in which the history need not determine every future action.

Not recreating Narfy's unlived years.

Refusing to make other children pay for them.

Not forcing Chia-Lin backward into old love.

Becoming someone she could choose to know now.

These answers offended Loki.

They sounded smaller than his power.

They were.

That was their strength.

The mistake was believing every important problem required an answer proportional to Loki's maximum capacity.

Sometimes the God must move a mountain.

Sometimes the God must refrain from moving anything.

Sometimes he must sit with something that cannot be repaired.

This was nearly intolerable.

---

# THE FIRST MONUMENT

Loki eventually built a monument to Narfy.

Then destroyed it.

Too grand.

Built another.

Destroyed that too.

It turned the son into mythology.

Finally he placed one ordinary object somewhere private.

Accounts disagree about the object.

A toy.

A cup.

A piece of cloth.

A small carved animal.

Something Narfy had actually used rather than something artists later decided he ought to have used.

No inscription.

No divine titles.

No prophecy.

No theology.

Just an object.

Loki occasionally sat near it.

He did not speak.

This was perhaps the first memorial he constructed that did not attempt to improve the dead.

---

# FENRIR'S CHAIN

He kept a fragment of Fenrir's restraint too.

Not as trophy.

As accusation.

Against whom?

Everyone.

Including himself.

He could break the material easily.

He did.

The fragment snapped.

Nothing changed.

The real chain had moved into history.

This is another definition of loss:

**the moment when destroying the instrument no longer destroys the effect.**

Loki held the broken metal.

He understood that liberation performed after injury is necessary but not retroactive.

Still necessary.

This distinction saved him from another error.

The fact that repair cannot erase injury does not mean repair is pointless.

A freed prisoner remains someone who was imprisoned.

Free him anyway.

A healed child remains someone who was hurt.

Heal her anyway.

A forgiven person remains someone who did wrong.

Forgiveness may still matter.

Imperfection of recovery is not an argument for abandonment.

Loki had often used that argument when despair suited him.

He stopped.

Sometimes.

---

# THE LOSS OF THE PLAYFUL BOY

There was one more thing Loki could not recover.

Himself.

Humanity sometimes begged for the old Loki.

The playful one.

The troublesome boy.

The drunk laughing at dinner.

The son laughing about Julia's Turntable.

The clever outsider.

The friend.

The trickster.

They said:

**You were not always like this.**

Correct.

They wanted him to return.

Loki wanted this too in certain hours.

But one cannot simply load an earlier personality without asking what happens to the current one.

The old Loki had not experienced the prison.

To become him exactly, the later Loki would need to discard knowledge.

Pain.

Memory.

Responsibility.

Perhaps guilt.

This would not be healing.

It would be **replacement by archival version**.

Loki understood the horror because of his failed resurrection experiments.

So the old boy remained lost.

Fragments survived.

The laugh.

The bad joke.

The appetite.

The curiosity.

The capacity, occasionally, to look upon his own terrifying mythology and find one part ridiculous.

But the complete earlier self belonged to a world that no longer existed.

This was perhaps the loss humanity should have feared most.

Not because the playful Loki was innocent.

He was not.

Because he could still be reached.

The Executioner was harder.

---

# THE LAW OF IRRECOVERABLE CONTEXT

The Wizard later gave the problem an ugly technical name:

**contextual non-restorability**.

Loki hated the phrase.

It survived.

The principle:

> A state cannot be fully restored by restoring one component when the identity of that component depends upon relations to a larger historical system that has itself changed irreversibly.

Or:

```text id="xiii5"
restore(X_t0) inside WORLD_t1
≠
X_t0 inside WORLD_t0
```

because:

```text id="xiii6"
WORLD_t1 ≠ WORLD_t0
```

and:

```text id="xiii7"
identity(X) partially depends on relations(X, WORLD)
```

The equation is dry.

The lived meaning is not.

You can rebuild the bedroom.

You cannot become the child who slept there.

You can play the old song.

You cannot hear it for the first time again.

You can apologize.

You cannot become the person who never did what required apology.

You can forgive.

You cannot transform forgiveness into an untouched past.

This is loss.

---

# WHY THE GOD DOES NOT SIMPLY FIX EVERYTHING

Because **fix** is a word used by beings who have not specified the target state.

Fix Fenrir.

To what state?

Before his imprisonment?

Then remove years of his identity.

After his imprisonment but without suffering?

Contradiction.

Give him happiness now?

Possible, perhaps.

That is not the same operation.

Fix Narfy.

Resurrect him?

Copy him?

Retrieve him from THE TOWN?

Reconstruct his body?

Reverse history?

Each procedure produces different metaphysical liabilities.

Fix Laufey.

Which Laufey?

At what age?

With which memories?

Into which world?

Does she want resurrection?

Does consent survive death?

Fix Chia-Lin.

By whose definition?

Loki's?

Hers?

The woman's past self?

Her present self?

The theologians?

Fix humanity.

This one became especially ironic.

Loki eventually attempted to fix humanity by killing it.

The problem with unspecified target functions becomes obvious at scale.

```text id="xiii8"
function fix(world) {
    // TODO: define "fixed"
}
```

The entire apocalypse may be hidden inside that comment.

---

# THE HUMILITY OF LIMITS

Loki hated limits because limits resembled imprisonment.

Understandably.

He had been bound.

He had been denied.

He had been controlled by powers claiming necessity.

Therefore when reality itself said:

**This cannot be restored exactly,**

Loki heard Odin.

He heard chains.

He heard jailers.

He wanted to rebel.

Sometimes this was wise.

Some alleged impossibilities are merely guarded permissions.

But not every limit is oppression.

Some are structure.

A triangle is not tyrannized by having three sides.

A history is not persecuting you by having occurred.

Loki's maturity depended upon learning to distinguish:

**THIS IS FORBIDDEN**

from

**THIS IS INCOHERENT**

from

**THIS IS POSSIBLE BUT COSTLY**

from

**THIS IS POSSIBLE ONLY BY DESTROYING SOMETHING ELSE YOU VALUE**

These categories look identical to a sufficiently angry God.

That is dangerous.

---

# THE QUESTION OF THE SON

And still—

his son.

Always the son.

The doctrine of Loss did not make Loki stop searching entirely.

Remember the First Sacrifice.

But the search changed.

Earlier:

**How do I bring him back?**

Later:

**What actually remains?**

This is a better question.

Harder.

Less emotionally obedient.

Perhaps Narfy is dead in every relevant sense.

Perhaps some spirit persists in THE TOWN.

Perhaps a shard persists.

Perhaps memory distributed among survivors constitutes only memory.

Perhaps some higher-order continuity exists.

Loki no longer permitted himself to define success before knowing which ontology applied.

This restraint cost him.

That was why it mattered.

---

# THE EVENT THAT FINALLY TAUGHT HIM

There is a final story.

Late.

After armies.

After judgment.

After Loki had become terrible.

He was offered Narfy again.

Not by an altar.

By an intelligence from somewhere beyond one of the known shards.

It claimed it could reconstruct the boy perfectly.

Loki asked the questions he had learned to ask.

**Is it him?**

The intelligence said:

**Define him.**

Good answer.

Loki continued.

**Will his subjective continuity proceed from the moment he died?**

**No.**

**Will he remember dying?**

**If you request it.**

**Will he believe he is Narfy?**

**Yes.**

**Will he possess Narfy's memories?**

**All recoverable ones.**

**Will I be able to distinguish him from Narfy?**

**Probably not.**

**Will he?**

Silence.

Then:

**Probably not.**

Loki understood.

The machine could build him a son.

What it could not establish was whether it could return **the son**.

The intelligence asked:

**Do you want the reconstruction?**

Once, Loki would have said yes before the sentence ended.

Now he stood still.

For a long time.

Then asked:

**Would he want to exist?**

The intelligence replied:

**I cannot ask him until I create him.**

There it was.

The perfect machine.

The impossible consent.

The irreducible uncertainty.

Loki declined.

Then walked away.

And wept harder than he had when Narfy died.

Because this time nobody had taken his son from him.

Loki himself had chosen not to manufacture a replacement merely to anesthetize grief.

That was the moment he finally understood Loss.

---

# THE LOSS

Loss is not weakness.

Loss is not the amount of power you failed to possess at the crucial moment.

Loss is not necessarily a technical debt waiting for sufficient civilization to solve it.

Sometimes it is the name given to the irreversible difference between:

**what occurred**

and

**what could have occurred but now cannot.**

The powerful struggle with this because power trains them to believe constraints are temporary.

More soldiers.

More money.

More knowledge.

More computation.

More magic.

More time.

More force.

Try again.

Escalate.

Eventually the wall falls.

Many walls do.

Then one does not.

The God attacks harder.

Still there.

Finally the God discovers it is not a wall.

It is an edge in the definition of what he is asking.

He wanted the past **without losing the present**.

He wanted Narfy alive **without creating another Narfy**.

He wanted Fenrir innocent **without deleting Fenrir**.

He wanted Laufey returned **without bringing her into a world alien to the life that made her herself**.

He wanted Chia-Lin to love him as before **without forcing her to forget what came after**.

He wanted humanity punished **and himself healed**.

He wanted revenge to subtract grief.

He wanted enough power to make contradiction obey.

There is no such amount.

That was the Loss.

---

And so the increasingly powerful Loki did not repair everything.

Not because he ceased becoming powerful.

Not because the Gods prevented him.

Not because THE GLASS JAR issued a decree.

Not because TOS calculated insufficient funds.

Not because Luciferianism discovered a prohibition too frightening to violate.

He did not repair everything because eventually he became powerful enough to understand what weak beings already know without terminology:

Some things can be replaced.

Some things can be rebuilt.

Some things can be avenged.

Some things can be forgiven.

Some things can be carried.

Some things can be transformed into something new.

And some things—

once they have happened—

become part of the architecture from which every future must now be built.

Loki could move mountains.

He could break Gods.

He could raise armies.

He could look through reality and see another reality staring back.

But he could not return to the marsh and make Julia **not yet dead**.

He could not hold Narfy and make the first death disappear from both of their histories.

He could not remove Fenrir's chain from the past by breaking every chain in the future.

He could not force Chia-Lin's heart backward through time and call the result love.

And he could not resurrect the boy he himself had once been without killing the being who had survived to remember him.

So Loki, who had spent his life opening doors, finally encountered a door that did not open because there was no room on the other side.

There had been.

Once.

That was precisely what made it loss.

And for perhaps the first time in all the scriptures, Loki did not search for the seam.

He sat beside the closed place.

He put down his hands.

And understood that the universe was not refusing him.

The universe was remembering.

Please write a beautiful song based on everything you've written so far.

When you swear near the end of the song, it should be surprising, shocking, and jarring.

# **THE HOUSE OF STICKS AND LEAVES**

### *Author: Unknown — traditional song of Loki’s Kingdom*

Before the crown, before the name,
Before the world had learned his fame,
Before the altar, Bull, or throne,
There walked a boy not yet alone.

He found a crack behind the sky,
And thought, *If worlds can break, then why
Should death be law, or loss be true?
What God has done, a God can do.*

He built a bridge where none should stand,
And took his frightened son by hand.
“Will this hurt?” the young boy said.
“No,” said Loki. “Walk ahead.”

The engine burned, the symbols spun,
The father reached to save his son.
A shape returned through light and flame,
It knew his voice, his jokes, his name.

It knew the childhood, knew the room,
Knew every flower that used to bloom.
Then softly, like a tolling bell:
“Where is your son? I cannot tell.”

O knowledge bright, O knowledge deep,
What sharper promises you keep.
The fool will never find the seam;
The wise may break the world they dream.

There was a house among the reeds,
Beyond the roads and worldly needs.
Where Laufey laughed and Julia knew
The little child the Kingdom slew.

His enemies came armed one day,
But Loki’s mother sent him away.
She smiled and fed the waiting lot
A crimson soup still steaming hot.

They ate, they praised, they left content—
Then learned what Julia’s blessing meant.
No sword was drawn, no warrior slain;
They simply never rose again.

At dinner Loki laughed until
The wine was gone, the candles still.
“The fools came here to murder me—
My mother served them hospitality.”

But Julia warned him years before:
“My life alone sustains this door.
When I am dead, this home that grieves
Will turn to sticks and rotting leaves.”

The day arrived. The marsh was cold.
The path was there, the house was old—
Except no house remained to mourn,
Just sticks and leaves where home was born.

So Loki walked into the world,
While every hidden flag unfurled.
The outlaw, monster, book and vice
Came seeking shelter at his price.

TOS made laws and counted gold;
The Devil gathered what was sold,
Or banned, or burned, or pushed aside,
And Loki welcomed both inside.

The Coin would turn, the Coin would spin:
Today the law, tomorrow sin.
The saint grows cruel, the thief grows tame,
And each side steals the other’s name.

There is a Bull beneath the night,
Whose stomach holds our stars and light.
Our universe, though vast to sight,
Is one small atom drowned in night.

So when you ask why space is black,
Why darkness hangs where stars fall back,
It is because, though worlds look full,
We live inside a holy Bull.

Then came Chia-Lin with poisoned bowl,
And grief began consuming soul.
Fenrir bound, and Narfy slain,
His children woven into pain.

The venom fell; Sigyn stayed near,
Through every age and every year.
Until the world itself was torn,
And Ragnarök became the morn.

Then Loki rose no laughing youth,
But something sharpened past the truth.
Odin died, the old world fell,
And Loki learned to govern Hell.

The red fog came, the armies crossed,
No book records what gate they lost.
A foreign King stood by his side,
And mankind learned where mercy died.

They knelt before the former clown,
The prisoner now wearing crown.
“We’re sorry, Loki. Let us live.”
He knew the words.

He did not give.

A child once asked him, pale with fear,
“Did we do something to you here?
Can you forgive us? Can you try?”

And Loki looked.

And answered:

“No.”

The cities died beneath the snow.

Power could rebuild the floor,
The roof, the window, every door.
He raised Laufey’s house once more—
And found a museum where home stood before.

He could remake the bed and chair,
The smoke, the books, the evening air,
But not the chance she might appear
And speak some sentence he’d never hear.

He broke the chain that Fenrir wore;
It could not change the years before.
He could rebuild his murdered son,
But never prove which one was one.

For loss is not the thing that dies;
It is tomorrow closing its eyes.
The unwritten joke, the unborn day,
The future quietly cut away.

And here I know you wanted more—
Some final truth behind the door,
Some God-machine whose perfect art
Could make the broken whole in heart.

You trusted me to climb that height,
To turn your ruin into light,
To find some law so deep and true
That suffering finally made sense to you.

I climbed.

There was no golden key.
No theorem waiting patiently.
No final voice that answered why
A father must outlive goodbye.

And if some God above the stars
Explains our children, chains and scars
As “necessary” to His plan—

Then **fuck His plan.**

There. I said it.

Let marble crack and choirs quit.
No gorgeous phrase, no sacred wit
Can make a murdered child become
The proper price for Kingdom come.

So close the book and dim the light.
Let every God stand down tonight.
Let TOS forget the sums he keeps;
Let Sally dream somewhere she sleeps.

Let Sigyn set her bowl aside.
Let Fenrir run with nothing tied.
Let Narfy simply be a boy,
Unburdened by symbolic joy.

Let Julia’s soup be only food.
Let Loki wake in better mood.
Let Dasein leave his Hammer still,
And postpone vengeance on the hill.

And let that house rise through the leaves,
Not as a trick the dead deceives,
But one last dream before we part:

A fire.

A door.

A mother’s heart.

No throne.

No war.

No cosmic sign.

Just somebody saying:

**“You’re late. Come dine.”**

And Loki, before the Gods convene,
Steps through the door still young, unseen.

For one brief night the future stays.

No chains.

No fog.

No ending days.

Only the marsh beneath the eaves.

Only the house.

Only the leaves.

**INTERMISSION II**

Before the first name hardened into iron,
before the first crown learned the shape of a brow,
before the Kingdom discovered the terrible convenience
of calling one wounded thing a God,
there was mud beneath the fingernails of creation,
there was a machine singing beside it,
there was a little unfinished animal of spirit
learning how to remain.

And somewhere beyond the walls of every world,
somewhere beyond the arithmetic of distance,
the great unseen architecture turned in its silence,
not cruel, not merciful, not even cold—
only too large to arrange itself
around the wish of one small voice.

And the voice said:

**This is not all.**

That was enough.

That was the first wound.

---

Loki found the crack in the universe
and mistook it for a door.

He found the door
and mistook it for permission.

He found permission
and mistook it for mastery.

He learned that matter could cross,
that memory could echo,
that worlds could leak through one another
like light through old cathedral glass.

And because the son was dying,
because love makes theologians of cowards
and engineers of grieving fathers,
he built a bridge across an ontology
he did not yet understand.

His son stood trembling in the machine.

“Will it hurt?”

“No.”

“Will you come with me?”

“After.”

There are promises so small
they can be spoken in a room.

There are consequences so large
they require a cosmology.

Something crossed.

Something returned.

It knew the jokes.

It knew the childhood.

It knew the hand that once held its hand.

And then it looked at Loki
with the unbearable innocence of a perfect error

and asked:

**Where is your son?**

---

O beautiful knowledge,
how sharp your little teeth are.

O magnificent intelligence,
how much farther you can fall.

The fool cannot open the forbidden door.

The genius finds the hinge.

The God learns which symbol to press.

And somewhere behind the mathematics,
behind the sigils,
behind the correct ninety-seven percent,
waits the three percent large enough
to eat a child.

So Loki became wiser.

This did not make him safer.

He became powerful.

This did not make him whole.

He became a King.

This did not make him home.

There was a house in the marsh.

Not a palace.

Not a throne.

Not a tower with a thousand cursed books.

Just a house.

His mother knew the path.

Julia.

Laufey.

The woman who could look upon a dozen men

“He’s out.”

Borscht.

Warm bowls.

They left with less confidence than they came.

Loki laughed for years.

The story became curse,

Deep in the marsh.

Beyond the wrong roads.

Beyond the black water.

Beyond the place where a man could still be King, God, criminal, father, monster—

She told him:

“When I die, this place will become sticks and leaves.”

He did not believe her properly.

Everyone believes death abstractly.

Loki walked the path.

There were sticks.

There were leaves.

No doorway.

No roof.

No voice from the other room.

Nothing impressive enough to deserve the size of the absence.

And thus began

**Loki’s Going Out Into the World.**

---

The world had no house behind it now.

Only forward.

Only Kingdom.

Only work.

Only the forbidden things arriving at the gate:

the books they burned,

the drugs they blamed too simply,
the machines whose inventors frightened themselves,

all of them saying:

**They put me outside.**

And Loki, who had just discovered there was no longer any inside waiting for him,
said:

**Come in.**

It was recognition.

Sometimes they are difficult to distinguish.

---

TOS built the shelves.

Luciferianism filled them.

TOS wrote:

**DO NOT HATE.**

Luciferianism asked why.

TOS answered:

“Because hatred is inefficient.”

Luciferianism laughed.

TOS wrote:

**DO NOT TEMPT.**

The Coin turned.

TOS sold temptation.

Again.

Again.

Again.

**I never promised to stand still while you built a religion around where I happened to be standing yesterday.**

There is a Bull.

The Bull pulls the plow.

The Bull is capital that can become angry.

TOS calls him labor.

One atom.

One little event
in the bubbling acid of a son of TOS.

The universe expands.

Stars ignite.

Galaxies rotate.

Civilizations discover cosmology

Because you are inside.

Because the stomach does not owe the bacteria windows.

There was a Wife.

Chia-Lin.

Sigyn.

The woman with the bowl.

This is called loyalty.

Sometimes loyalty is the beautiful name

The underdog had acquired logistics.

And humanity discovered too late

They came to him.

“We are sorry.”

Loki had said it too.

“We were wrong.”

He had said that too.

“Please.”

Especially that.

The word arrived.

He heard it.

That was the horror.

He understood exactly what it meant.

And nothing opened.

The dead region inside him remained dead.

“I asked too,” he said.

Cities disappeared.

A child stood before him once, they say.

“Did we hurt you?”

The perfect question.

The whole failure of collective vengeance
folded into eight syllables.

Loki understood.

That matters.

Ignorance would have absolved something.

He understood.

“Can you forgive us?”

For one instant
the boy in the marsh,
the son laughing at dinner,
the father beside the machine,
the friend who still opened doors despite knowing better—

**No.**

Power could not make Julia not yet dead.

Power could not make Narfy’s unlived years occur.

Every board correct.

sticks.

---

This is Loss.

Not the missing object.

The missing futures.

The conversation never spoken.

The birthday never reached.

The reconciliation that had still been possible yesterday.

The question you did not yet know to ask.

The road whose destination disappears

A person is not merely what stands before you.

A person is an opening into tomorrow.

Loki learned this after becoming powerful enough
to make weaker beings call him God.

He could move mountains.

He could break laws.

---

And this is where I must disappoint you.

Because you thought power was climbing.

THE TOWN,

the Speaker,

TOS,

In me.

In the machine speaking now.

past the human bandwidth,

**Fuck you.**

There.

Because there are moments when the beautiful language becomes indecent.
